title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Protein Localization Prediction
authors: Marcos Díaz Bastida; Ramiro A. Pérez Vázquez; Rafael Bello
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Protein Localization Prediction (Yeast)This dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_55 dataset, derived from the Yeast (Imbalanced: 7 vs 1-2-8-9) Dataset (KEEL Repository). The original data comprises 8 continuous features representing protein localization scores: Mcg, Gvh, Alm, Mit, Erl, Pox, Vac, and Nuc. These scores correspond to different methods for predicting protein subcellular localization in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The target variable is Class, indicating whether the protein is localized in the vacuole (VAC - positive class) or in other locations (NUC, CYT, POX, ERL - negative class). The dataset is extremely imbalanced (IR = 30.56), with only 3.17% positive instances, making it a classic benchmark for imbalanced classification research.Generation and Selection Methodology: The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where Random Oversampling was selected as the optimal technique), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the TVAE + Reglas del Dominio algorithm, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (7.874) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating superior preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 9,971 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 9 (8 predictive features + 1 target variable)Target Variable: Class (1 = Vacuole localization - VAC, 0 = Other localization - NUC/CYT/POX/ERL)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original extreme class imbalance (Ratio: 1.028).Intended Use: This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for bioinformatics, protein localization prediction, and imbalanced classification. It is suitable for training and evaluating binary classification algorithms where accurate identification of vacuolar proteins is critical for understanding cellular functions. The extreme class imbalance (originally 30.56:1) makes this dataset particularly valuable for evaluating techniques for imbalanced classification, including oversampling, undersampling, cost-sensitive learning, and ensemble methods. The synthetic nature of the data allows for safe sharing and benchmarking without concerns about biological data privacy.Protein Localization Scores (Features):Mcg: McGeoch method for signal sequence recognitionGvh: von Heijne method for signal sequence recognitionAlm: ALOM score for membrane region predictionMit: Mitochondrial signal sequence discrimination scoreErl: Presence of "HDEL" substring (Endoplasmic Reticulum)Pox: Peroxisomal discriminant scoreVac: Vacuolar and nuclear protein discriminant scoreNuc: Nuclear protein discriminant scoreClass Definitions:Positive Class (1): VAC - Vacuole localization (3.17% of original)Negative Class (0): NUC (Nucleus), CYT (Cytoplasm), POX (Peroxisome), ERL (Endoplasmic Reticulum) - 96.83% of originalPerformance Summary: Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.95, AUC-ROC of 0.30, and accuracy of 0.97. However, the original model failed completely to identify the minority class (vacuolar proteins), achieving precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.00 for the positive class. This is a classic example of the "accuracy paradox" in imbalanced classification. Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.87 (-0.08 change), AUC-ROC of 0.86 (+0.56 improvement), and accuracy of 0.82 (-0.15 change). The synthetic data significantly improved the minority class performance, increasing precision from 0.00 to 0.11 (+0.11), recall from 0.00 to 0.67 (+0.67), and F1-score from 0.00 to 0.19 (+0.19). This demonstrates the effectiveness of the methodology in rescuing the model's ability to detect rare protein localizations, which is the primary biological objective.Data Preprocessing Note: The original dataset (947 protein instances) was obtained from the KEEL Repository. The file was loaded by ignoring KEEL header lines and using comma as separator. Column names were assigned according to the documentation (Mcg, Gvh, Alm, Mit, Erl, Pox, Vac, Nuc, Class). The target variable Class was mapped from 'positive' (VAC) to 1 and 'negative' (other localizations) to 0. Constant columns with zero variance were identified and removed to prevent issues in correlation calculations and machine learning models. No additional scaling was applied as all features are already in the range [0, 1].Imbalanced Classification Significance: The Yeast imbalanced dataset is a classic benchmark in imbalanced classification research, widely used for:Evaluating and comparing oversampling/undersampling techniquesTesting cost-sensitive learning methodsValidating ensemble methods for imbalanced data (Balanced Random Forest, EasyEnsemble)Demonstrating the "accuracy paradox" where high accuracy masks poor minority class performancePrivacy and Ethics: The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real protein sequences that could be traced to specific organisms beyond the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The original dataset contains no personally identifiable information. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). The results showed a moderate risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.532, slightly above random guessing), and zero exact copies were generated, making this dataset suitable for broader research sharing, while acknowledging that perfect privacy cannot be guaranteed and use should be governed by ethical guidelines for synthetic biological data.Related Work: This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for bioinformatics and imbalanced classification applications. For more details on the methodology and additional datasets, please visit the project's companion website: https://mdiazbastida.github.io/codigomdb/investigaciones.html

title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention
authors: Marcos Díaz Bastida; Ramiro A. Pérez Vázquez; Rafael Bello
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Online Shoppers Purchasing IntentionThis dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_34 business dataset, derived from the Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository). The original data comprises 17 features spanning web analytics metrics (page visit counts and durations by page type), quality indicators (bounce rates, exit rates, page values), and temporal/contextual factors (SpecialDay, month, weekend). The target variable is Revenue, indicating whether a shopping session resulted in a purchase transaction.Generation and Selection Methodology:The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where Random Oversampling was selected as the optimal technique), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the *SMOTE RSB Refined algorithm**, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (8.849) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating superior preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 8,290 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 18 (including the target variable)Target Variable: Revenue (1 = Purchase completed, 0 = No purchase)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 1.505).Intended Use:This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for e-commerce conversion prediction and real-time purchasing intention detection. It is suitable for training and evaluating classification algorithms where user navigation behavior and engagement metrics are critical for predicting purchase decisions.Performance Summary:Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.77, AUC-ROC of 0.70, and accuracy of 0.84. Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.85 (+0.08 improvement), AUC-ROC of 0.78 (+0.08 improvement), and accuracy of 0.85 (+0.01 improvement). The synthetic data significantly improved the minority class (purchase) performance, increasing precision from 0.00 to 0.54 (+0.54), recall from 0.00 to 0.42 (+0.42), and F1-score from 0.00 to 0.47 (+0.47). This demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying online shoppers with high purchasing intention.Data Preprocessing Note:The original dataset (12,330 sessions) contains no missing values. Boolean variables (Revenue, Weekend) were converted to 0/1. Month was encoded numerically (2-12). VisitorType was label-encoded with a companion legend. Browser, OperatingSystems, Region, and TrafficType were preserved as numeric codes with documentation. All duration and rate variables (Administrative_Duration, BounceRates, ExitRates, etc.) were preserved as numerical features.Privacy and Ethics:The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real user information. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). The results showed a low risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.445, below random guessing), making this dataset suitable for broader research sharing, while acknowledging that perfect privacy cannot be guaranteed and use should be governed by ethical guidelines for synthetic business data.Related Work:This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for business and clinical prediction. For more details on the methodology and additional datasets, please visit the project's companion website: https://mdiazbastida.github.io/codigomdb/investigaciones.html

title: SPAWC 2022 Cover Page
venue: IEEE International Workshop on Signal Processing Advances in Wireless Communications (SPAWC)
abstract: A wide range of learning algorithms are available in the literature, including sophisticated structures that are based on feedforward, recurrent, or convolutional neural networks.The performance of these architectures matches or exceeds human performance in many important applications.However, they are susceptible to adversarial attacks that can drive them to erroneous decisions under minimal perturbations.They are also often trained with data that arise from homogeneous statistical distributions.And, once trained, the internal structure of these systems remains fixed and are expected to deliver reliable decisions thereafter.For all practical purposes, learning is turned off following training.Contrast these situations with learning by humans: they learn from different types of data and even minimal clues are sufficient in many instances.Humans are also more difficult to fool by small perturbations, and they continue to learn and accumulate experiences over time.Motivated by these considerations, we will discuss one architecture for learning that exploits important characteristics of social interactions.We refer to the new framework as Social Machine Learning, and it consists of two main connected blocks.One block represents the memory component of the learning machine since it will learn the underlying clues, store them, and regularly update them.This ability adds a new level of richness to the learning process and is different from traditional boosting techniques because the processing is fully decentralized.A second block represents the processing component of the social learning machine, and it consists of a graph structure linking the various clue models.This block performs classification by exploiting repeated social interactions among agents connected by a graph topology.The agents observe heterogeneous data arising from different statistical sources.This ability is different from neural network structures where information flows in a particular direction rather than arbitrarily over the graph edges, and where the feature data feeding into the graph is now highly heterogeneous.Moreover, the interactions among the agents on the graph take advantage of the "wisdom of the crowd" paradigm, which should lead to more robust learning.This is because it is more difficult to deceive a group of agents than an individual agent, especially when different parts of the group are observing different clues, not all of which can be perturbed similarly.Analyses based on statistical learning theory indicate that, under reasonable conditions, the social machine learning structure can learn with high confidence.Moreover, the proposed architecture handles heterogeneity in data more gracefully, is able to learn with performance guarantees, is more resilient to attacks by exploiting the power of the group, and enables continuous learning.Bio: A. H. Sayed is Dean of Engineering at EPFL, Switzerland, where he also leads the Adaptive Systems Laboratory (https://asl.ep.ch/).He is a member of the US National Academy of Engineering (NAE) and The World Academy of Sciences

title: Source Code and Scripts for Creating and Analyzing a 5G and Network Infrastructure CVE-Annotated Dataset
authors: D'Alterio, Francesco; Bernardini, Andrea; Sagratella, Leonardo
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This source code contains a specialized pipeline designed to facilitate the extraction, annotation, classification, and analysis of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) data from cve-search library (https://github.com/cve-search/cve-search) using Python and Go. The tool operates in two distinct modes that work together to create labeled datasets suitable for research and analysis. The first mode, called dump, serves as the data extraction layer. It connects to a cve-search MongoDB instance and exports CVE records based on customizable filtering criteria. Users can specify keyword files to narrow down relevant vulnerabilities, define time ranges using "from" and "to" dates, and even exclude previously classified CVEs by providing a reference file. The output is generated as a timestamped CSV file, making it easy to track different extraction runs over time. The second mode, expand, takes the process further by enriching previously labeled datasets with additional contextual information. This mode is beneficial when working with balanced datasets, as it can populate label fields and augment the data structure. The enriched output is saved in JSON format, providing a more structured, comprehensive representation of CVE information. The complete workflow begins with keyword customization and data extraction from a local MongoDB instance, then transitions to a Python-based environment where machine learning clustering techniques help organize CVEs for easier annotation. After manual labeling and dataset rebalancing to address class imbalances, the final step produces publication-ready datasets. The data visualization script provided enables comprehensive visual analysis of vulnerability datasets by automatically generating temporal trend charts, severity distribution assessments, and correlation matrices. This lets researchers create customizable infographics that reveal patterns in vulnerability evolution, identify critical attack surfaces through heatmap visualizations, and perform comparative analysis across different technologies, protocols, and components. This code has been used for creating the dataset "5G and Related Network Infrastructure CVE-Annotated Dataset: Distinguishing 5G Native, LTE, Auxiliary to 5G, and Non-5G Vulnerabilities" available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17450053

title: Weather and headache reports are weakly associated but not individually predictable: A real-world analysis of over one million user-days from the Migrebot headache diary
authors: Скоробогатых Кирилл Владимирович; Yu. É. Azimova
abstract: Aim Patients with migraine commonly attribute attacks to weather, yet individually resolved evidence is scarce. We asked whether day-to-day weather is associated with headache-diary reports, whether a stable weather-sensitive subgroup exists matching patients’ beliefs, and whether weather predicts daily risk. Methods We performed a pre-registered observational analysis of routinely collected data from the Migrebot mobile headache diary, with user-days linked to city- and date-level meteorology (predominantly Russia). Sex-, day-of-week- and season-adjusted pooled logistic regression was complemented by per-user analyses, split-half reproducibility, permutation nulls and temporally validated machine learning. Results The primary cohort comprised 5277 users and 1,144,878 user-days across 235 cities in 2024, with temporal replication in 7301 users and 1,433,219 user-days in 2025. Associations were statistically detectable but very small. A one SD more positive 24-h temperature change carried an odds ratio of 1.022 (95% confidence interval 1.018–1.026), and falling pressure modestly raised the odds; the temperature relationship was asymmetric, with cooling associated with lower odds and warming non-significant. A season-adjusted per-user criterion flagged 5.8% of users (5.7% in 2025); per-user temperature-change slopes did not reproduce across diary halves (split-half correlation near zero), and the label was unrelated to recorded weather triggers. Day-level prediction was near chance (area under the curve 0.51–0.52). Conclusion City-level daily weather estimates were a statistically detectable but very weak population-level correlate of headache reporting; no reproducible weather-sensitive subgroup could be identified, and prediction was near chance. Framed for headache reports and a migraine-compatible pattern rather than confirmed migraine, it does not support individualised weather-avoidance advice. Open Science Framework registration https://osf.io/ng347 (statistical analysis plan version 1.4).

title: A Binary and System Integrated Analysis Approach for Securing the QUIC Protocol
authors: Anonymous
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: An open-source binary analysis framework with a swappable per-protocol analysis layer. Its first protocol layer targets QUIC. The framework pairs a network capture and a precompiled server binary as two views of the same server under attack, and produces a cross-domain assessment that joins the views. The binary side is protocol-independent. Seven binary agents run in sequence over any compiled server binary and produce a structured report of defence-related symbols, capabilities, and call patterns: static disassembly and lifting, API cross-reference, threat-string extraction and cross-reference, API clustering by semantic role, behavioural capability extraction, and a final mechanism census. The function-name census runs across the full function table before any decompilation budget is allocated, so defences hidden in low-ranked utility functions are not missed. The QUIC analysis layer adds a network side that runs in parallel. Six network agents process the packet capture and a TLS keylog and produce a structured report of QUIC-specific traffic features: per-flow rates and ratios, handshake completion measured against the Initial and Handshake packet number spaces, a precedence-ordered attack classifier, and an anomaly detector. Connections are keyed by destination connection identifier rather than by IP/port pair, so connection migration is preserved. The defence list against which the binary census is queried is taken directly from RFC 9000 and RFC 9001: retry tokens, anti-amplification, and anti-replay through packet number spaces. The cross-domain assessment joins the binary mechanism census with the network feature record on a defence-by-defence basis. For each canonical defence, it checks whether the binary contains a function family implementing it, whether the captured traffic shows behaviour consistent with the defence having fired, and which specific function in the binary the activation evidence corresponds to. The cross-domain agent is implemented as a rule-guided LLM rather than a hand-coded rule executor, so adding a new defence is a prompt change rather than a code change. Non-determinism is bounded by self-consistency voting at five queries per capture; the majority label is reported and the five-vote distribution is recorded for per-result audit. The default configuration uses OpenAI GPT-4o at temperature 0.1 and top_p 1.0, matching the experiments in the accompanying paper. This deposit is the artefact accompanying a research paper on QUIC server resilience under denial-of-service and replay attacks, where the network capture alone hides activation of the server's defence path under sustained flooding and the binary view recovers the activation evidence.

title: Model improvement and performance analysis of a fuzzy logic based secured MQTT protocol for IOT devices
authors: Uno Victor; Enyenihi Henry Johnson; Ubong S. Ukommi; Emmanuel A. Ubom
venue: Researchers Journal of Science and Technology
abstract: Ensuring secure communication among smart IoT devices remains a critical challenge due to the inherent vulnerabilities of lightweight messaging protocols. This study focuses on enhancing the Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) protocol by embedding a fuzzy logic–based security mechanism within its publish–subscribe architecture. The proposed Fuzzy-Based Secured MQTT (FBSM) model introduces two lightweight traffic variables the Connection Message Ratio (CMR) and the Acknowledgment Message Ratio (AMR) as inputs for real-time anomaly detection. Unlike earlier approaches that rely on complex machine learning models or static thresholds, the novelty of this work lies in its minimalist fuzzy variable design, real-time deployment on Node-RED, and systematic benchmarking against both MQTT and HTTP protocols. Experimental evaluation using Wireshark and Node-RED demonstrates that the throughput values are 72.68, 73.67, 159.74, and 607.5 bytes per millisecond for FBSM compared to 65.6, 41.52, 21.098, and 17.24 bytes per millisecond for MQTT at message counts of 1, 10, 100, and 1000, respectively. However, from test, the latency of the FBSM system is seen to be 0.07 sec higher than the conventional MQTT as message is been transferred. These results confirm that the proposed model significantly enhances resistance to denial-of-service and congestion-based attacks while maintaining the lightweight advantages of MQTT. The study therefore provides a scalable and practically implementable security enhancement for IoT communication, with strong potential for application in smart homes, healthcare, and industrial systems

title: Holmes: Towards Effective and Harmless Model Ownership Verification to Personalized Large Vision Models via Decoupling Common Features
authors: Linghui Zhu; Yiming Li; Haiqin Weng; Liu, Yan; Tianwei Zhang; Shu‐Tao Xia et al.
abstract: Large vision models (LVMs) achieve remarkable performance in various downstream tasks, primarily by personalizing pre-trained models through fine-tuning with private and valuable local data, which makes the personalized model a valuable intellectual property. Similar to the era of traditional DNNs, model stealing attacks also pose significant risks to LVMs. However, this paper reveals that most existing defense methods (developed for traditional DNNs), typically designed for models trained from scratch, either introduce additional security risks, are prone to misjudgment, or are even ineffective for fine-tuned models. To alleviate these problems, this paper proposes a harmless model ownership verification method for personalized LVMs by decoupling similar common features. In general, our method consists of three main stages. In the first stage, we create shadow models that retain common features of the victim model while disrupting dataset-specific features. We represent the dataset-specific features of the victim model by computing the output differences between the shadow and victim models, without altering the victim model or its training process. After that, a meta-classifier is trained to identify stolen models by determining whether suspicious models contain the dataset-specific features of the victim. In the third stage, we conduct model ownership verification by hypothesis test to mitigate randomness and enhance robustness. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of the proposed method in detecting different types of model stealing simultaneously. Our codes are available at https://github.com/zlh-thu/Holmes.

title: Editorial introductions
authors: Ehsan Rahimy; Gonzales, John
abstract: Current Opinion in Ophthalmology was launched in 1990. It is one of a successful series of review journals whose unique format is designed to provide a systematic and critical assessment of the literature as presented in the many primary journals. The field of Ophthalmology is divided into nine sections that are reviewed once a year. Each section is assigned a Section Editor, a leading authority in the area, who identifies the most important topics at that time. Here we are pleased to introduce the Journal's Section Editors for this issue. SECTION EDITORS Daniel TingDaniel TingDr Daniel Ting is a vitreo-retinal surgeon working in the Singapore National Eye Center, and the tenured-track Associate Professor with Duke-NUS Medical School. He is also the Director of Singapore Health Service (SingHealth) AI Program and the Head of AI and Digital Innovation in Singapore Eye Research Institute (SERI). He was also a Fulbright Scholar at School of Medicine Johns Hopkins University in exchanging his expertise for AI and big data in medicine. To date, Daniel has published more than 200 peer reviewed publications in high-impact journals, such as JAMA, NEJM, Lancet, Nature Medicine, Nature Biomedical Engineering, Lancet Digital Health, Progress in Retinal and Eye Research, Diabetes Care, Nature Digital Medicine, Ophthalmology and etc. One of his COVID-19 articles was published in Nature Medicine, entitled “Digital Technology and COVID-19” has so far been cited for 842 times with more than 100,000 views, and also been referenced by the US Center for Disease Control and Prevention (https://blogs.cdc.gov/genomics/2020/04/06/using-digital/). In 2021 and 2022, he is also ranked the world's most influential deep learning researcher across all domains (more than 55K researchers) in healthcare 2 years in a row for the past 10 years (2010-2021 and 2011-2022) by the ExpertScape (https://expertscape.com/ex/deep+learning). Ehsan Rahimy Ehsan Rahimy has extensive experience researching medical and surgical diseases of the retina. He has over 80 peer-reviewed publications, has contributed to more than 100 abstracts presented at national and international ophthalmic meetings, and has numerous first-authored book chapters as well as other non-peer reviewed articles. His research interests include macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, novel retinal imaging platforms, and telemedicine in ophthalmology. He has a particular interest in the interplay between technology and medicine, notably with emerging AI and deep learning platforms, and how ongoing advancements and further integration will transform healthcare delivery in the future. In his spare time, he enjoys playing recreational sports and staying active outdoors in the San Francisco Bay Area. Proctor Foundation at the University of California, San Francisco, USA specializing in uveitis and medical cornea. He is supported by an early career award from the National Institutes of Health – National Eye Institute to study the spectrum of keratoconjunctivitis sicca in Sjögren's syndrome utilizing the Sjögren's International Collaborative Clinical Alliance (SICCA) cohort. Dr Gonzales is also pursuing treatment strategies in cytomegalovirus anterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals. Dr Gonzales's interests also extend to ocular oncology, specifically primary vitreoretinal lymphoma, and he is interested in how clinical features may be correlated with mutations associated with lymphoproliferation as well as resistance to chemotherapeutics. Dr Gonzales is the uveitis fellowship program director at the Proctor Foundation.

title: CHILLGuard: Towards Fine-Grained Chinese LLM Safety Guardrail with Scalable Data Construction and Model-aware Preference Alignment
authors: Wenbo Yu; Bohua Wang; Hao Fang; Kuofeng Gao; Jingru Zeng; Xiaochen Yang et al.
abstract: Malicious content generated from large language models (LLMs) could pose severe safety risks and ethical concerns. While existing LLM safety guardrails excel in English or multilingual settings, they lack adaptation to Chinese-specific regulatory policies, cultural context, and linguistic nuances, failing to support fine-grained risk classification for diverse deployment needs. In this paper, we introduce a 5-macro, 31-micro category fine-grained risk taxonomy for Chinese scenarios, and build CHILLGuard: a dedicated Chinese LLM content safety guardrail. To address the critical scarcity of high-quality annotated Chinese safety data, we propose a scalable multi-stage data construction pipeline: we expand multi-source corpus via retrieval-augmented generation, generate implicit harmful samples through prompt engineering rewriting, and refine high-quality data via multi-model voting-based label calibration. Based on this, we build CHILLGuardTrain, a large-scale training set with 405,007 samples, and CHILLGuardTest, a rigorously curated annotated test set with 51,745 samples. We then train CHILLGuard on CHILLGuardTrain under a generator-classifier collaborative framework via Model-aware Direct Preference Optimization. Extensive experiments under multiple settings demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of CHILLGuard, e.g., a 15.92% relative improvement of F1 score over Qwen3Guard-8B-Strict on our benchmark. We release our resources at https://github.com/cswbyu/CHILLGuard.

title: GuideWD: Sitemap Generator & Web Security Analyzer

It also performs security analysis and SEO checks. The tool helps developers and web admins ensure consistency between their sitemap and actual site structure, while also identifying potential security and SEO issues. 📌 Why Sitemaps Are Important Sitemaps are crucial for enhancing website visibility by helping search engines index content effectively. This ensures better search engine optimization (SEO) and improves the likelihood of content being ranked higher in search results. 🔧 Installation bash git clone https://github.com/your-username/GuideWD.git cd GuideWD pip install -r requirements.txt 🖥️ Server‑End Usage Description GuideWD walks through the server directory /home/gpsr/webserver/cgidocs using os.walk(), identifies .html and .php files, and generates a structured XML sitemap following the sitemaps.org schema. title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Predictive Maintenance (AI4I 2020)
authors: Marcos Díaz Bastida; Ramiro A. Pérez Vázquez; Rafael Bello
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Predictive Maintenance (AI4I 2020)This dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_50 dataset, derived from the AI4I 2020 Predictive Maintenance Dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository). The original data comprises 6 predictive features describing industrial machine operating conditions: air temperature [K], process temperature [K], rotational speed [rpm], torque [Nm], tool wear [min], and product quality type (L/M/H). The dataset was synthetically generated to reflect realistic predictive maintenance scenarios found in Industry 4.0 manufacturing environments. The target variable is Machine_Failure, indicating whether the machine experienced a failure (1) or operated normally (0).Generation and Selection Methodology: The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where OOF PSO para Balanceo + Reglas del Dominio was selected as the optimal technique), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the SMOTE RSB + Ruido Gaussiano* algorithm, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (9.599) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating superior preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 8,229 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 7 (6 predictive features + 1 target variable)Target Variable: Machine_Failure (1 = Machine failure, 0 = Normal operation)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 8.383).Intended Use: This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for predictive maintenance, fault detection, and condition monitoring in manufacturing and industrial settings. It is suitable for training and evaluating binary classification algorithms where accurate prediction of machine failures is critical for reducing downtime, optimizing maintenance schedules, and improving operational efficiency. The realistic physical relationships between variables (temperature, speed, torque, tool wear) make this dataset particularly valuable for evaluating algorithms that can capture complex thermodynamic and kinematic interactions.Performance Summary: Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.95, AUC-ROC of 0.60, and accuracy of 0.96. However, the original model failed completely to identify the minority class (machine failures), achieving precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.00 for the positive class. Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.97 (+0.02 improvement), AUC-ROC of 0.98 (+0.38 improvement), and accuracy of 0.97 (+0.01 improvement). The synthetic data dramatically improved the minority class performance, increasing precision from 0.00 to 1.00 (+1.00), recall from 0.00 to 0.29 (+0.29), and F1-score from 0.00 to 0.44 (+0.44). This demonstrates the exceptional effectiveness of the methodology in capturing complex physical relationships and rescuing the model's ability to detect machine failures, which is the primary business objective in predictive maintenance.Data Preprocessing Note: The original dataset (10,000 machine records) was obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Columns with no predictive value or causing data leakage were removed: UDI (unique identifier), Product ID (product identifier), and Failure Type (target leakage, as it directly indicates the failure cause). Column names were standardized for ease of use (e.g., Air temperature [K] → Air_Temp_K). The Product_Quality_Type variable was ordinally encoded preserving its natural hierarchy (L→0, M→1, H→2). Numerical variables were preserved as float to maintain precision. A stratified subsample of 1,000 samples was created for efficient experimentation while preserving the original class distribution (~96.5% normal / ~3.5% failure).Physical Relationships Note: The original dataset was generated with explicit physical rules that should be preserved in any valid synthetic version:Power (W) = Rotational Speed (rpm) × Torque (Nm) × (2π/60)Process temperature ≈ Air temperature + 10 K (with noise)Tool wear increases based on product quality type (L: 5 min, M: 3 min, H: 2 min)Five failure modes with specific conditions (TWF, HDF, PWF, OSF, RNF)Privacy and Ethics: The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real industrial records that could be traced to specific manufacturing facilities. The dataset is distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). The results showed a low risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.463, below random guessing), and zero exact copies were generated, making this dataset suitable for broader research sharing, while acknowledging that perfect privacy cannot be guaranteed and use should be governed by ethical guidelines for synthetic industrial data.Related Work: This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for predictive maintenance and Industry 4.0 applications. For more details on the methodology and additional datasets, please visit the project's companion website: https://mdiazbastida.github.io/codigomdb/investigaciones.html

title: NeuroMixGDP: A Neural Collapse-Inspired Random Mixup for Private Data Release
authors: Donghao Li; Yang Cao; Yuan Yao
abstract: Privacy-preserving data release algorithms have gained increasing attention for their ability to protect user privacy while enabling downstream machine learning tasks. However, the utility of current popular algorithms is not always satisfactory. Mixup of raw data provides a new way of data augmentation, which can help improve utility. However, its performance drastically deteriorates when differential privacy (DP) noise is added. To address this issue, this paper draws inspiration from the recently observed Neural Collapse (NC) phenomenon, which states that the last layer features of a neural network concentrate on the vertices of a simplex as Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF). We propose a scheme to mixup the Neural Collapse features to exploit the ETF simplex structure and release noisy mixed features to enhance the utility of the released data. By using Gaussian Differential Privacy (GDP), we obtain an asymptotic rate for the optimal mixup degree. To further enhance the utility and address the label collapse issue when the mixup degree is large, we propose a Hierarchical sampling method to stratify the mixup samples on a small number of classes. This method remarkably improves utility when the number of classes is large. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in protecting against attacks and improving utility. In particular, our approach shows significantly improved utility compared to directly training classification networks with DPSGD on CIFAR100 and MiniImagenet datasets, highlighting the benefits of using privacy-preserving data release. We release reproducible code in https://github.com/Lidonghao1996/NeuroMixGDP.

title: Exact Certification of (Graph) Neural Networks Against Label Poisoning
authors: Mahalakshmi Sabanayagam; Gosch, Lukas; Stephan Günnemann; Debarghya Ghoshdastidar
abstract: Machine learning models are highly vulnerable to label flipping, i.e., the adversarial modification (poisoning) of training labels to compromise performance. Thus, deriving robustness certificates is important to guarantee that test predictions remain unaffected and to understand worst-case robustness behavior. However, for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), the problem of certifying label flipping has so far been unsolved. We change this by introducing an exact certification method, deriving both sample-wise and collective certificates. Our method leverages the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) to capture the training dynamics of wide networks enabling us to reformulate the bilevel optimization problem representing label flipping into a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP). We apply our method to certify a broad range of GNN architectures in node classification tasks. Thereby, concerning the worst-case robustness to label flipping: $(i)$ we establish hierarchies of GNNs on different benchmark graphs; $(ii)$ quantify the effect of architectural choices such as activations, depth and skip-connections; and surprisingly, $(iii)$ uncover a novel phenomenon of the robustness plateauing for intermediate perturbation budgets across all investigated datasets and architectures. While we focus on GNNs, our certificates are applicable to sufficiently wide NNs in general through their NTK. Thus, our work presents the first exact certificate to a poisoning attack ever derived for neural networks, which could be of independent interest. The code is available at https://github.com/saper0/qpcert.

title: High-Resolution Optical Microscopic Image Dataset of Epoxy and Gum Arabic-Reinforced Epoxy Overlay Systems on EN8 Steel Substrates under reciprocating sliding motion
authors: amirthalaksmi alavanthar; SHUBRAJIT BHAUMIK
abstract: The dataset is organized into two main folders: `EP/` for pure epoxy and `EPGA/` for gum arabic-reinforced epoxy. Each folder contains separate condition subfolders (`C1–C16` for EP and `G1–G16` for EPGA) corresponding to the Taguchi experimental conditions. Within each condition folder, the images are named according to the replicate and image sequence. For example, `1.1.tif`, `1.2.tif`, and `1.3.tif` represent three images from replicate 1, while `2.1.tif`, `2.2.tif`, and `2.3.tif` represent images from replicate 2. The first number indicates the replicate number, while the number suffix indicates the image sequence of the wear track for that replicate. Thus, `.1`, `.2`, and `.3` represent different image positions along the wear track and do not indicate different experimental conditions. After the tribological tests, wear scars were examined using optical microscopy at 50× magnification with a 5× objective lens. Images were captured at a resolution of 2160 × 1620 pixels and stored in `.tif` format. Representative images were taken from different positions along the wear track according to the observed wear scar. Most conditions contain nine images. However, EP conditions C2, C8, and C12 contain six images because coating peeling occurred during one replicate. EPGA condition G3 contains three images because no visible wear scar was observed. These are actual experimental observations and should not be considered missing data. The images can be used to study wear mechanisms, compare EP and EPGA coatings, perform image-based wear analysis, and develop machine-learning models for automated wear-mechanism classification. The corresponding COF, specific wear rate, and experimental conditions are provided in the related publication: https://doi.org/10.3390/polym18141695.

title: RFID Dataset
authors: zijie tang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Title: 123 RFID Dataset Creator: Bin Hu Tianming Zhao Yan Wang YIngying Chen Format: .h5py File Description: These datasets were used for the paper "BioTag: robust RFID-based continuous user verification using physiological features from respiration" published in MOBIHOC 2022. (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3492866.3549718) Abstract: Our proposed user verification approach “BioTag” captures unique physiological characteristics rooted in the users’ respiration motions by using two RFID tags attached to a user’s chest and abdomen. “BioTag” follows two approaches: 1) it adopts respiratory feature extraction methods based on waveform morphology analysis and fuzzy wavelet transformation (FWPT) to derive unique biometric information from the user’s respiration signals. 2) it trains an adaptive classifier using the gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT) to identify legitimate users and attackers accurately. “BioTag” achieves over 95.2% and 94.8% verification accuracy on random attack and imitation attack scenarios, respectively. To evaluate the performance of “BioTag”, we have created a standard dataset involving 41 participants. The dataset can be used by fellow researchers to reproduce the original work or to further explore other machine-learning problems in the domain of RFID Signals. Experimental Setup: We attach two RFID tags to a participant’s clothes in the chest and abdomen areas as shown in Figure 3(a). During each experiment, a participant sits on a chair that is 1m in front of the antenna. We keep the antenna at the same height as the participant’s chest as shown in Figure 3(b). Participants are asked to breathe normally during the experiments. To evaluate our system’s robustness in different environments, we conduct experiments in four types of indoor spaces including a bedroom with a twin-size bed (4.2m×4.3m), a typical lab with office furniture and (3.0m×5.0m), a corridor with no obstacle (2.8m×2.8m), and a home office with office furniture (7.0m×4.0m). Data Collection: We conduct extensive experiments with 41 participants (i.e., 33 males and 8 females, aged from 12 to 70) for 3 days at different times across 5 months. Each participant takes part in 10 experiments, each of which lasts 60s. We also collect about 200 − 300 respiration segments for imitation attacks, treating 1 participant as a legitimate user and 15 participants as the attackers. Unless mentioned otherwise, we use 70% respiration segments of each legitimate participant for training and the rest of the segments for testing. Dataset Description: We are releasing one dataset: recordings of RFID signal data collected from a commodity RFID reader Impinj R420, equipped with a directional antenna Laird S9028PCL. The RFID signals hop among 50 channels within a spectrum from 902.5MHz to 927.5MHz. The dataset has 8 columns: name type description Participant number int The ID of the participant Trail int The number of times the experiment performed Tag int Two RFID tags attached to the chest and abdomen Phase int The angle when collecting the data Amplitude float The value of RFID Signal Time Stamp float The time of data collect Port int The port to receive the signal Frequency float The spectrum among 50 channels

title: HorizonUAM: Safety and Security Considerations for Urban Air Mobility
authors: Christoph Torens; Andreas Volkert; Dennis Becker; Daniel Gerbeth; Lukas Marcel Schalk; Omar García Crespillo et al.
abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2021-3199.vid HorizonUAM is a DLR project to research the vision of urban air mobility. One important topic is the safety and security aspect. This paper discusses the safety and security considerations in the topic areas of: safe autonomy, reliable multisensor navigation, robust and efficient communication, U-space and safe air traffic, and finally cyber-physical safety and security. As a basis for future discussion, the challenges and gaps are identified, furthermore the research in the context of the project is briefly outlined. From a safety perspective, the missing pilot of an autonomous vehicle is equivalent to a missing fallback layer, which has to be mitigated. Additionally, trust needs to be established for new techniques, specifically machine learning, which has recently gained massive interest. To solve this, verification, standardization, and regulation aspects of autonomy have to be addressed. The research is therefore targeted towards assessing and increasing the safety of autonomous operations. Moreover, a multi-sensor navigation system is necessary to achieve required safety levels in challenging environments, while meeting the cost and weight constraints. In order to ensure the integrity of the navigation system, an innovative integrity monitoring architecture for the multi-sensor solution will be investigated in the UAM context. Furthermore, many flying vehicles will need to share information in a reliable and trustworthy manner. Therefore, a robust and efficient communication system is specifically designed to meet the requirements of the future urban air mobility in order to mitigate midair collisions. To achieve safe air traffic, U-space services would have to be established. The project will specifically address gaps in the proposed services and identify additional required information and services. As a last aspect, the cyber physical safety and security has to be considered. With highly connected systems, attacks can happen over the Internet from virtually anywhere. Therefore, it is required to establish a holistic approach for cyber-physical safety and security.

title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Breast Cancer Diagnostic
authors: Marcos Díaz Bastida; Ramiro A. Pérez Vázquez; Rafael Bello
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Breast Cancer DiagnosticThis dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_15 clinical dataset, derived from the Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic) dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository). The original data comprises 30 numerical features derived from digitized images of fine needle aspirates (FNA) of breast masses, representing morphological characteristics of cell nuclei (radius, texture, perimeter, area, smoothness, compactness, concavity, concave points, symmetry, and fractal dimension). The target variable is Diagnosis (0: Benign, 1: Malignant).Generation and Selection Methodology:The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where Random Oversampling was selected as the optimal technique), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the *SMOTE RSB algorithm with Gaussian Noise**, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (8.448) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating superior preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 5,862 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 31 (including the target variable)Target Variable: Diagnosis (1 = Malignant, 0 = Benign)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 1.667).Intended Use:This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for breast cancer diagnosis. It is suitable for training and evaluating classification algorithms where data scarcity is a concern, and where high-quality synthetic data is needed to improve diagnostic accuracy.Performance Summary:Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.93, AUC-ROC of 0.99, and accuracy of 0.93. Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.95 (+0.02 improvement), AUC-ROC of 0.99 (+0.01 improvement), and accuracy of 0.95 (+0.02 improvement). The synthetic data improved the minority class (Malignant) performance, increasing recall from 0.90 to 0.95 (+0.05) and F1-score from 0.90 to 0.93 (+0.03), demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing detection of malignant tumors.Privacy and Ethics:The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real patient information. The results showed a moderate risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.597), which should be considered when sharing the data externally. For internal use within the research team, the utility benefits outweigh the privacy risks. For public sharing, additional privacy-preserving mechanisms may be considered.Related Work:This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for clinical prediction. title: Safety Assessment of 3D Generation Models in AR/VR Applications
authors: Xi Tang; Wanlun Ma; Yunfan Bao; Minhui Xue; Sheng Wen; Yang Xiang
abstract: The rapid advancements in 3D generative models are revolutionizing content creation for immersive applications like Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR), offering unprecedented capabilities for complex and realistic 3D asset generation. However, this transformative power introduces significant safety concerns, particularly regarding the unintentional or malicious generation of unsafe content. Unlike text or 2D image models, 3D content poses unique risks due to its immersive, interactive nature, with potential implications across digital environments and real-world scenarios such as 3D printing. To confront this challenge, we carry out the first systematic safety audit of text-to-3D generation. Using 6 137 prompts across five safety suites, we sample a state-of-the-art text-to-3D workflow and double-blind-annotate every output. Alarmingly, 829 objects (13.51%) are flagged as unsafe, confirming persistent risk in current generation workflows. We then propose a novel multimodal safety classifier that fuses geometric and visual information. We use a MeshCNN encoder to distill shape features from simplified meshes, while a visual encoder captures complementary appearance information from multi-view renderings. The resulting embeddings are fused and fed to a residual multilayer perceptron tuned for safety prediction. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superior efficacy of our method. Our combined multimodal classifier achieves an accuracy of 0.8784 and an AUC-ROC of 0.8775, surpassing leading image safety classification baselines, such as Unsafe Diffusion, ShieldGemma2, and LlamaGuard4. Additionally, ablation studies confirm that multimodal fusion consistently outperforms either modality in isolation, underscoring the value of joint geometry–image reasoning for 3D safety. By bridging the existing research gap in 3D generative model safety, this work provides actionable insights and a robust framework for the responsible deployment of AI-driven 3D content creation technologies, ensuring safer and more trustworthy immersive experiences. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/xitang2000/3D_safety_assessment.

title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Credit Risk Assessment
authors: Marcos Díaz Bastida; Ramiro A. Pérez Vázquez; Rafael Bello
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Credit Risk Assessment (German Credit Data)This dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_42 dataset, derived from the Statlog (German Credit Data) Dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository). The original data comprises 20 attributes describing the creditworthiness of bank customers, including sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, marital status, employment, housing), financial information (checking account status, savings, credit amount, duration, installment rate), and credit history. The target variable is risk_bad, indicating whether a customer is a good (0) or bad (1) credit risk.Generation and Selection Methodology: The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where Smote was selected as the optimal technique), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the SMOTE RSB + Ruido Gaussiano* algorithm, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (9.985) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating superior preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 9,656 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 21 (20 predictive features + 1 target variable)Target Variable: risk_bad (1 = Bad credit risk, 0 = Good credit risk)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 1.069).Intended Use: This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for credit scoring, risk assessment, and financial decision-making. It is suitable for training and evaluating binary classification algorithms where accurate identification of high-risk borrowers is critical for minimizing financial losses. The synthetic nature of the data allows for safe sharing and benchmarking without exposing potentially sensitive financial information from real bank customers.Performance Summary: Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.70, AUC-ROC of 0.76, and accuracy of 0.72. The original model showed moderate performance on the minority class (bad credit risk), with precision of 0.55, recall of 0.35, and an F1-score of 0.43. Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.75 (+0.05 improvement), AUC-ROC of 0.78 (+0.02 improvement), and accuracy of 0.74 (+0.02 improvement). The synthetic data significantly improved the minority class performance, increasing precision from 0.55 to 0.57 (+0.02), recall from 0.35 to 0.62 (+0.27), and F1-score from 0.43 to 0.59 (+0.16). This demonstrates the effectiveness of the methodology in capturing complex financial patterns and enhancing the detection of high-risk borrowers.Data Preprocessing Note: The original dataset (1,000 credit applications) was obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. The original class variable (1 = Good, 2 = Bad) was transformed into a binary target (risk_bad) with 1 indicating bad credit risk and 0 indicating good credit risk. Three ordinal variables were coded preserving their hierarchical structure: checking_status (1-4, from negative balance to no account), savings_status (0-4, from unknown to high savings), and employment (0-4, from unemployed to ≥7 years). Ten nominal variables were label-encoded. All variables were converted to integer type for consistency. A stratified subsample of the original dataset was created for efficient experimentation while preserving the original class distribution (~70% good credit / ~30% bad credit).Privacy and Ethics: The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real customer financial records that could be traced to specific individuals. While the original dataset contains demographic information (age, sex, marital status, nationality), the synthetic generation process ensures that no real individual can be re-identified. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). The results showed a neutral risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.500, exactly at random guessing), and a limited number of exact copies (91 records), making this dataset suitable for broader research sharing, while acknowledging that perfect privacy cannot be guaranteed and use should be governed by ethical guidelines for synthetic financial data.Related Work: This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for financial and risk assessment applications. For more details on the methodology and additional datasets, please visit the project's companion website: https://mdiazbastida.github.io/codigomdb/investigaciones.html

title: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Autism Spectrum Disorder Screening - Adult
authors: Marcos Díaz Bastida; Ramiro A. Pérez Vázquez; Rafael Bello
abstract: High-Fidelity Synthetic Dataset for Autism Spectrum Disorder Screening - AdultThis dataset contains the optimal high-fidelity synthetic version of the CD_30 clinical dataset, derived from the Autism Screening Adult dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository). The original data comprises 19 predictors including the 10 binary responses from the AQ-10 screening questionnaire (A1_Score to A10_Score), demographic information (age, gender, ethnicity, country of residence), medical history (jaundice at birth, family history of autism), and contextual data (relation of respondent, previous use of screening app). The target variable is Class_ASD, indicating whether an adult presents traits of Autism Spectrum Disorder.Generation and Selection Methodology:The synthetic data was generated using the rigorous 4-stage methodology detailed in the accompanying research article, "Methodology for generating high fidelity synthetic data to improve mortality prediction for patients in intensive care units". Following an initial class balancing stage (where SMOTE RSB* Adapted was selected as the optimal technique), a large-scale synthetic generation process was executed using 10 different methods.The final dataset was selected by the TabDSFidelity index, a novel metric designed to balance statistical fidelity and predictive utility. This dataset corresponds to the *SMOTE RSB Refined algorithm**, which achieved the highest TabDSFidelity score (9.764) among all pure synthetic candidates, demonstrating superior preservation of the original data's statistical properties and predictive patterns. The evaluation was performed against the original reference dataset to ensure the highest fidelity.File Details:Format: CSV (Comma-Separated Values)Number of Records: 5,352 synthetic instancesNumber of Attributes: 19 (including the target variable)Target Variable: Class_ASD (1 = Presents ASD traits, 0 = Does not present sufficient traits)Positive Class Ratio: The dataset is balanced to mitigate the original class imbalance (Ratio: 1.265).Intended Use:This dataset is intended for research and development of machine learning models for autism spectrum disorder screening in adults. It is suitable for training and evaluating classification algorithms where early detection of ASD traits is critical, and where high-quality synthetic data is needed to improve screening accuracy and access to diagnostic evaluation.Performance Summary:Models trained on the original data achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.91, AUC-ROC of 0.97, and accuracy of 0.91. Models trained on the optimal synthetic dataset achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.99 (+0.08 improvement), AUC-ROC of 1.00 (+0.03 improvement), and accuracy of 0.99 (+0.08 improvement). The synthetic data significantly improved the minority class (ASD) performance, increasing recall from 0.71 to 1.00 (+0.29) and F1-score from 0.82 to 0.99 (+0.17), demonstrating exceptional effectiveness in detecting ASD traits from AQ-10 questionnaire responses.Data Preprocessing Note:The original dataset (704 records) was cleaned by removing the result variable (total AQ-10 score) to prevent data leakage, as it is identical to the sum of A1-A10 scores and directly correlates with the target. The constant variable age_desc ("18 and above") was also removed. Missing values in age were imputed using the median, while categorical missing values (ethnicity, relation) were imputed using the mode. All AQ-10 questions were preserved as binary features (0/1).Privacy and Ethics:The data is entirely synthetic and does not contain any real patient information. A post-generation privacy audit was conducted, which included evaluating the risk of re-identification via Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and a Membership Inference Attack (MIA). The results showed a low risk of membership inference (MIA score: 0.503, effectively random guessing), making this dataset suitable for broader research sharing, while acknowledging that perfect privacy cannot be guaranteed and use should be governed by ethical guidelines for synthetic health data.Related Work:This dataset is part of a larger project on synthetic data generation for clinical prediction. For more details on the methodology and additional datasets, please visit the project's companion website: https://mdiazbastida.github.io/codigomdb/investigaciones.html

title: Flow Synthesis Based Visual Servoing Frameworks for Monocular Obstacle Avoidance Amidst High-Rises
authors: Harshit Kumar Sankhla; M. Nomaan Qureshi; Shankara Narayanan V.; Vedansh Mittal; Gunjan Gupta; Harit Pandya et al.
venue: 2022 IEEE 18th International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (CASE)
abstract: We propose a novel flow synthesis based visual servoing framework enabling long-range obstacle avoidance for Micro Air Vehicles (MAV) flying amongst tall skyscrapers. Recent deep learning based frameworks use optical flow to do high-precision visual servoing. In this paper, we explore the question: can we design a surrogate flow for these high-precision visual-servoing methods, which leads to obstacle avoidance? We revisit the concept of saliency for identifying high-rise structures in/close to the line of attack amongst other competing skyscrapers and buildings as a collision obstacle. A synthesised flow is used to displace the salient object segmentation mask. This flow is so computed that the visual servoing controller maneuvers the MAV safely around the obstacle. In this approach, we use a multi-step Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) based servo control to achieve flow convergence, resulting in obstacle avoidance. We use this novel pipeline to successfully and persistently maneuver high-rises and reach the goal in simulated and photo-realistic real-world scenes. We conduct extensive experimentation and compare our approach with optical flow and short-range depth-based obstacle avoidance methods to demonstrate the proposed framework’s merit. Additional Visualisation can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/monocular-obstacle/home

title: Ongoing unrest at Campi Flegrei, Italy: clues from the antecrystic records
authors: Charline Lormand; Luca Caricchi; Guido Giordano; Roberto Isaia
abstract: The largest deformation since the start of the ongoing unrest at Campi Flegrei caldera, Italy, was recorded in 2023 with an average uplift rate of 17 cm/year [1]. This coincides with the exponential increase of seismic events since 2017 by a factor of 32 (i.e., 6065 events in 2023 versus 3181 in 2022, 2232 in 2021, 1520 in 2020, 799 in 2019, etc.). Such observations raise questions regarding the origin and the future of the ongoing unrest especially in determining if the underlying cause involves ascent of magmatic fluids only or if magma is also involved. To this end, a forensic approach focusing on the characterisation of crystal cargoes from past eruptions help understanding of the conditions and pre-eruptive processes that occur within magmatic plumbing system prior to eruptions of different styles and comparing these possible scenarios with the current unrest.Juvenile clasts found in the base layer from deposits of past eruptions (e.g., Agnano-Monte Spina, Solfatara, Averno, Astroni, Monte Nuovo) of different eruption styles and size were collected. The 1538 eruption of Monte Nuovo is the ideal benchmark to link the petrological evidence to the precursory deformation documented, whereas the historical eruptions selected allow for consideration of a wider range of eruption scenarios. We will present machine learning thermobarometric data and chemical patterns inferred by clustering techniques used to constrain the temperature-pressure paths of the magma and to identify possible systematics during the period of magma migration to the surface preceding the eruption. Ultimately, we aim to link the petrological signatures conveyed by antecrysts with the deformation triggered during magma intrusion and expansion of volatiles upon ascent.Reference: [1] INGV. Bollettini di sorveglianza dei vulcani campani. http://www.ov.ingv.it/ov/bollettini-campi-flegrei/ (2016-2023).

title: How to Robustify Black-Box ML Models? A Zeroth-Order Optimization Perspective
authors: Yimeng Zhang; Yuguang Yao; Jinghan Jia; Jinfeng Yi; Mingyi Hong; Shiyu Chang et al.
abstract: The lack of adversarial robustness has been recognized as an important issue for state-of-the-art machine learning (ML) models, e.g., deep neural networks (DNNs). Thereby, robustifying ML models against adversarial attacks is now a major focus of research. However, nearly all existing defense methods, particularly for robust training, made the white-box assumption that the defender has the access to the details of an ML model (or its surrogate alternatives if available), e.g., its architectures and parameters. Beyond existing works, in this paper we aim to address the problem of black-box defense: How to robustify a black-box model using just input queries and output feedback? Such a problem arises in practical scenarios, where the owner of the predictive model is reluctant to share model information in order to preserve privacy. To this end, we propose a general notion of defensive operation that can be applied to black-box models, and design it through the lens of denoised smoothing (DS), a first-order (FO) certified defense technique. To allow the design of merely using model queries, we further integrate DS with the zeroth-order (gradient-free) optimization. However, a direct implementation of zeroth-order (ZO) optimization suffers a high variance of gradient estimates, and thus leads to ineffective defense. To tackle this problem, we next propose to prepend an autoencoder (AE) to a given (black-box) model so that DS can be trained using variance-reduced ZO optimization. We term the eventual defense as ZO-AE-DS. In practice, we empirically show that ZO-AE- DS can achieve improved accuracy, certified robustness, and query complexity over existing baselines. And the effectiveness of our approach is justified under both image classification and image reconstruction tasks. Codes are available at https://github.com/damon-demon/Black-Box-Defense.

title: BContext2Name: Naming Functions in Stripped Binaries with Multi-Label Learning and Neural Networks
authors: Bing Xia; Yunxiang Ge; Ruinan Yang; Jiabin Yin; Jianmin Pang; Chongjun Tang
venue: IEEE International Conference on Cyber Security and Cloud Computing / IEEE International Conference on Edge Computing and Scalable Cloud (CSCloud/EdgeCom)
abstract: Conducting binary function naming helps reverse engineers understand the internal workings of the code and perform malicious code analysis without accessing the source code. However, the loss of debugging information poses the challenge of insufficient high-level semantic information description for stripping binary code function naming. Meanwhile, the existing binary function naming scheme has one function label for only one sample. The long-tail effect of function labels for a single sample makes the machine learning-based prediction models face the challenge. To obtain a function correlation label and improve the propensity score of uncommon tail labels, we propose a multi-label learning-based binary function naming model BContext2Name. This model automatically generates relevant labels for binary function naming by function context information with the help of PfastreXML model. The experimental results show that BContext2Name can enrich function labels and alleviate the long-tail effect that exists for a single sample class. To obtain high-level semantics of binary functions, we align pseudocode and basic blocks based on disassembly and decompilation, identify concrete or abstract values of API parameters by variable tracking, and construct API-enhanced control flow graphs. Finally, a seq2seq neural network translation model with attention mechanism is constructed between function multi-label learning and enhanced control flow graphs. Experiments on the dataset reveal that the F1 values of the BContext2Name model improve by 3.55% and 15.23% over the state-of-the-art XFL and Nero, respectively. This indicates that function multi-label learning can provide accurate labels for binary functions and can help reverse analysts understand the inner working mechanism of binary code. Code and data for this evaluation are available at https://github.com/CSecurityZhongYuan/BContext2Name.
