from a given hash function30 Collision resistance Computationally infeasible for two distinct inputs to result in the same hash output23 APPLICATIONS OF BLOCKCHAIN TECHNOLOGY Apart from application in finance, blockchain technology could be highly relevant in other industries such as health care, insurance, and supply chain management4 due to the inherent key advantages: immutable transaction records, decentralized peer-to-peer transaction, costless verification, reduction of incumbent market power, avoidance of single point of failure, and smart contracts – automated executions of complex transactions based on computational logic. Although it has yet to achieve mass-market adoption, blockchain technology has been heavily touted as a potential general-purpose technology, gaining traction across multiple industries such as finance, hedge fund management, and supply chain management.4 Years of reliance on antiquated digital systems have resulted in cumbersome, inefficient and resource-intensive processes. This results in significant resource wastage, and also renders systems susceptible to fraudulent attacks or system-wide failure.5 Financial institutions are therefore innovating with blockchain technology to address these concerns. Another frontrunner in the adoption of blockchain technology is supply chain management.6–8 The complex multi-faceted nature of supply chains places heavy demands on proper record keeping, quality control, and transaction monitoring. Current supply chains rely on centralized intermediation entities with little transparency across the entire chain. The supply chain thus suffers from vulnerability towards malicious modification or human errors and poor accountability. The application of blockchain technologies has the potential to disrupt the industry by effectively eliminating the trust required between involved parties. By transferring the onus of trust onto the algorithm and its immutable record, the issues associated with the need of verifying intermediaries can be eliminated.9 BLOCKCHAIN TECHNOLOGY IN HEALTH CARE In a 2019 technical report by International Telecommunication Union,10 the Telecommunication Standardization Sector identified the health care sector as one of the key sectors that could be a beneficiary of blockchain technology. The devastating COVID-19 pandemic, while unfortunate, has provided a significant impetus to accelerate this process.11 It is important to note that traditional distributed database management system (DDMS) can support the secure transfer of health data through encryption and data masking with the acceptance of several significant flaws: potential single point of failure, subject identification and tampering of data. In comparison, blockchain armed with asymmetric encryption and hash values can surmount these challenges albeit with a measured sacrifice of throughput rate and latency. At this point, adoption of blockchain in health care is still in its infancy with multiple proof of concepts but a limited selection of commercially available health care blockchain platforms. At present, most of these platforms are focused on electronic medical record management, such as patient-controlled electronic medical record (EMR) accessibility and immutable recording of clinical records. One of the most well-known is Medicalchain (Medicalchain SA, London) which is built on the Hyperledger Fabric architecture. Medicalchain's12 primary focus is to assign EMR access-granting rights to the patient, thereby returning control back to the patient. It provides a self-contained incentive system by rewarding data-sharing behavior with its native token (MedToken) which can be utilized in exchange for relevant services. Another example is the national rollout of the e-Estonia health care EMR built on Keyless Signature Infrastructure blockchain technology, allowing for verification of integrity of accessed medical records as well as immutable record of access logs.13 Since its inception in 2016, it has enabled digital permeation with 99% of health data digitized securely and handling up to 1.8 million patient queries every month, made possible through decentralized authenticated sharing of data. Notable examples of data sharing on the e-Estonia platform include physician retrieval of time-critical patient information during emergencies as well as patient monitored access of their medical data.14 Separately, blockchain could potentially be a disrupting technology in the health care supply chain and insurance field. The decentralized nature of blockchain provides a platform for cross-institution and cross-border collaboration, providing transparent check and balance to all stakeholders. This gave rise to initiatives such as Pharmaledger—a European Union blockchain consortium involving 12 global pharmaceutical firms such as Pfizer, Novartis and GSK.15 In the health care insurance field, peer-to-peer transaction of cryptographically-secured sensitive information between stakeholders would remove costly intermediaries and improve efficacy. Fraudulent activities would also be deterred by the algorithm and the immutable log. This could transform the entire patient-customer journey, from verifiable health declaration during policy purchase to transparent and traceable claims process. It is thus becoming apparent that the trust-less verification and immutable audit trail afforded by blockchain is exceedingly crucial for innovative applications in health care. BLOCKCHAIN TECHNOLOGY IN OPHTHALMOLOGY Ophthalmology as a field has been an early adopter of new evolving technologies, in particular the application of AI and deep learning (DL) for the automated analysis of medical images, such as retinal images and optical coherence tomography scans.16–18 DL in medicine (and ophthalmology), an area of active research, is highly reliant on the availability of large high-quality datasets as well as rigorous model validation and testing. However, the management of diverse datasets from different countries and centers for training and testing of algorithms in these studies poses significant challenges. This is attributable to extensive restrictions due to concerns over data security and patient confidentiality, preventing honest transfer of research medical data to support collaborative efforts.19 In addition, proper research community oversight over the multitude of novel AI and DL systems is unattainable due to a lack of transparency regarding model validation and testing. Recognizing these challenges, in a recent study, Tan et al20 proposed a permission blockchain-enabled platform (based on Hyperledger Fabric) to assist with the development and validation of DL algorithms to tackle the global myopia epidemic. They provide proof-of-concept, using this blockchain-enabled platform for secure handling of data transfer, model sharing, and auditable reporting of model validation and testing results across 3 separate sites in 2 countries, in the development of robust DL algorithms for automated detection of myopic macular degeneration and high myopia from retinal images. They suggest that this blockchain-based solution for the management of research datasets and model testing results provides advantages of data integrity and immutability, as well as automation in data consistency and a shared ledger promoting easier collaboration. They also suggest that widespread adoption of this novel method could increase validity and transparency of AI studies in medicine, and may allow health regulators (eg, US Food and Drug Administration) a means of effectively auditing and verifying the diagnostic performance of AI algorithms for regulatory approval. In conjunction, the immutable transaction log replicated across all nodes provides the ideal digital infrastructure to track each iteration of the AI-model training, improving collaborative efficiency and trust. Further applications of blockchain in the health care industry could likewise impact the field of ophthalmology (Table 2). Supply chain transformation is particularly valuable for perishable products21 and would likely play a significant role in health care, where tight monitoring of labile high-value medications is crucial to guarantee safety and efficacy. Scarce or costly products that require highly regulated storage conditions would be ideal candidates, examples which include total parenteral nutrition, mRNA COVID vaccines, intra-vitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factors (anti-VEGF), blood products or biologics. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Lin et al established a blockchain-based platform to provide virtual clinical service for ophthalmology patients. They proposed a proof-of-concept to verify and efficiently monitor online prescriptions, creating a blockchain-based online pharmacy for prescription renewals and remote drug delivery.22 The significance of this lies in the fact that telemedicine is a highly visual-dependent service, making it particularly well-suited for visual-oriented specialties like ophthalmology. Another potential application of blockchain in health care, which will be highly relevant in ophthalmology, is the use of blockchain technology to monitor and improve patient treatment adherence as well as to automate medication support programs. This would be particularly valuable for high-cost treatment regimes that require considerable patient compliance, such as recurring intra-vitreal anti-VEGF treatments. TABLE 2 - Blockchain Characteristics and Potential Use Case Immutability31–38 AI algorithm training and testing, health care insurance, data transfer, medication distribution supply chain, patient support programme, medical licensing, patient disease monitoring, clinical drug trial Traceability and provenance31,32,34,37,39 Data transfer, medication distribution supply chain, patient support programme, medical licensing De-centralized data security33–37 Patient support programme, health care insurance, patient disease monitoring, data transfer Peer to peer transaction31–35,37 Health care insurance, data transfer, patient support programmes Cost-less verification33,35,37–40 Health care insurance, patient disease monitoring, patient support programmes, medication distribution supply chain, clinical drug trial Smart contracts/De-centralized autonomous organisations33,35,40,41 Medication distribution supply chain, patient support programmes, health care insurance, Anonymity31,32 Data transfer, patient support programme CHALLENGES Although we expect greater innovative and disruptive use cases for blockchain technology in ophthalmology to materialize, implementation and integration could remain a challenge. First, selecting the appropriate blockchain platform will be critical which, under most health care circumstances, will exclude permissionless blockchains. Researchers, clinicians, and hospital administrators will need to be cognizant of the clinical and operational workflow changes required if blockchain is adopted. Second, mindsets deeply rooted in the traditional DDMS will need to be changed. In addition, switching from DDMS to blockchain will entail greater digital automation, integration of application programming interfaces (API) and distributed applications (Dapps), off and on-chain event connection, wholesale conversion to digitized data collection and upgrading of the information technology infrastructure. Third, there are significant costs. Investments will be required for dedicated digital hardware, networking and storage overheads as well as maintenance. Fourth, from a clinician and provider perspective, immutability of the blockchain platform will prevent amendments of erroneous entries whereas latency could be a source of frustration when contrasted against highly efficient traditional client-server databases. Fifth, blockchain relies on a flawless algorithm to create an asymptotic security, hence cryptographic flaws could leave vulnerabilities within the platform. Finally, data security issues need to be addressed. The decentralized peer-to-peer transaction could potentially compromise patient's data if it has not been appropriately anonymized. The sensitive nature of health care data hence demands that the algorithm undergo extensive trials and penetration tests to guarantee that the patient's privacy and confidentiality is upheld. Finally, the democratization of data sharing at the patient-level might not materialize. It is highly possible that the lure of incentives would be nullified by heightened senses towards privacy preservation, hence failing to convince and motivate patients to proactively share their data. Such inertia could be further compounded by a lack of understanding and trust of the reliability of blockchain platforms. It might be more realistic to consider monetization of big data in an institutional level, yet even that faces significant resistance for fear of privacy breaches or the loss of autonomy over valuable data (Supplementary table: https://links.lww.com/APJO/A87). CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS In conclusion, the health care sector faces a pressing need for new digital technologies that allow secure and efficient sharing of data to address the inefficiencies and demands in current systems. There is increasing recognition that blockchain technology could deliver the novel digital platforms that are required to address these requirements. In the field of ophthalmology, blockchain technology can help to monitor data and results integrity, greater research to support AI In addition, and algorithms are likely to further improve the and of blockchain for widespread health care applications care.

title: Plasma proteins can tell your biological organs’ age (including the heart)
authors: Daniela Pedicino; Giovanna Liuzzo
abstract: Comment on ‘Organ aging signatures in the plasma proteome track health and disease’ which was published in Nature, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06802-1. The authors measured organ-specific aging in living individuals by assessing plasma levels of specific proteins originating from 11 different organs. Using machine learning models, they estimated organ age in five independent prospective longitudinal cohorts: Covance, LonGenity, Stanford Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (Stanford-ADRC), Stanford Aging Memory Study (SAMS), and Knight Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (Knight-ADRC).1 The study included a total number of 5676 subjects, who were followed for as long as 15 years. Age spanned from 19 to 104 years in the five cohorts (mean age, 70 years), with 55% females and 81% Whites. The researchers first analysed 4979 proteins. By using the Gene Tissue Expression Atlas (GTEx) human tissue bulk RNA-seq database, they identified organ-specific genes and plasma proteins. A gene or protein was called ‘organ-specific’ or ‘organ-enriched’ if its expression was four-fold higher in one organ compared with any other organ. A total of 893 (18%) proteins fulfilled the organ-enriched criterion, with the highest number for brain proteins. Following quality control, 4778 proteins (856 organ-enriched, 18%) were used for further analyses. They trained an ‘organismal’ aging model using the 3907 organ-nonspecific plasma proteins as inputs to compare the contribution of specific organs to an organ-shared aging signature and a ‘conventional’ proteomic aging model using all 4778 proteins to compare the organ aging models to a global plasma proteomic aging signature. This led to 11 organ-specific aging models, which were firstly trained in 1398 healthy adults from the Knight-ADRC cohort and then tested/validated using blood samples from the other >4000 subjects of the five cohorts. For each individual, the aging model produced a measure of his/her biological age based on the molecular profile compared with other same-aged peers, named ‘age gap’. The analysis was restricted to adipose tissue, artery, brain, heart, immune tissue, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, and pancreas, due to their contribution to aging and accessibility to age-related phenotypic information in the cohorts. Cardiac aging proteins were chosen among those expressed primarily by cardiomyocytes and with a known role in heart biology and disease, such as pro-brain natriuretic peptide and troponin T. Other less characterized heart proteins included cardiac myosin light chain, peroxidasin-like, and bone morphogenetic protein 10. Individuals with the same conventional ‘age gap’ displayed different organ age gap profiles, and some individuals had extreme aging in one or more organs as compared with the general population. The study identified extreme agers (extreme aging types, e-ageotypes), defined by a 2 SD increase or decrease in at least one age gap. The relationships between organ age and biological aging, testing the association between organ e-ageotypes and nine age-related disease states (Alzheimer’s disease, atrial fibrillation, cerebrovascular disease, heart attack, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia, hypertension, obesity, and gait impairment), were investigated and showed links between organ age differences and outcomes, such as heart failure and all-cause mortality. The authors found that 18% of the population had an organ-specific e-ageotype characterized by significantly accelerated aging in one organ (2.0% heart agers and 2.0% kidney agers), and ∼1.7% had multi-organ aging. Organ-specific diseases were associated with faster aging of particular organs (e.g. individuals with hypertension or diabetes had kidneys older than their same-aged peers, and subjects with atrial fibrillation or heart attack had hearts >2 years older). Accelerated organ aging (1 SD of additional age, corresponding to ∼4 year extra age) increased mortality risk by 15%–50%. Similarly, 4 years of additional heart age conferred a 2.5-fold increased risk of heart failure over a 15-year follow-up. Accelerated brain and vascular aging independently predicted Alzheimer’s disease development, being additive with other validated biomarkers such as plasma pTau-181. Chronological age is a recognized risk factor for morbidity and mortality. However, biological processes underlying aging are characterized by substantial heterogeneity, which implies that subjects with the same chronological age may show different risks for age-associated diseases and different health outcomes.2 Not only individuals but also organs, tissues, and cells may age in different ways throughout the lifespan. Cellular senescence has been studied in depth in cardiovascular disease to characterize the mechanisms underlying atherosclerosis development and progression.3,4 The accumulation of senescent cells in the arterial walls may contribute to chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, key features of atherosclerosis, from its onset to the development of acute cardiovascular events and eventually heart failure.5,6 These aspects, together with the increasing rate of the world’s aging population, justify the search for reliable indicators of biological age, rather than chronological age, which may track the underlying mechanisms, thus providing a better predictor of lifespan and a potential target to slow down the aging process. Advances in basic research have increased the variety of potential biomarkers that may be considered hallmarks of aging, and previous studies have already demonstrated that aging varies between individuals through the assessment of epigenetic markers.7–11 A significant acceleration of the epigenetic age has been associated with the presence, extension, and progression of subclinical atherosclerosis in middle-aged asymptomatic individuals regardless of traditional cardiovascular risk factors.12 However, the causal relationship between biomarkers and biological age is still a matter of debate. The study of Oh et al. provides substantially novel information on organ aging in a large population, spanning the adult lifespan and different age-related diseases. By analysing nearly 5000 plasma proteins in blood samples of >5500 individuals, it represents one of the most comprehensive approaches to understanding aging processes and how they intersect with diseases for which aging acts as a major risk factor. One of the major strengths of the study is the potential applicability of the findings in a real-world scenario, where an approach requiring a small blood sample may allow identifying organ-specific proteins involved in accelerated organ aging and increased disease risk. Alongside, the information coming from the model might be potentially used before the development of clinical manifestations, to guide early therapeutic interventions. From a practical standpoint, this approach may completely revolutionize the treatment of diseases such as heart failure and Alzheimer’s, both associated with high morbidity and mortality and heavy economic burden, by shifting the target of treatment towards a preventive, rather than a curative, strategy. However, caution should be used in interpreting the data, since the study included Caucasian-skewed cohorts of mostly older adults and focused on specific organs (including blood vessels). Thus, it remains unclear whether the described approach may be generalized to other populations or other organs. Moreover, it is not clear whether the proteins represent the key players in the aging process or its by-products. Some therapeutic approaches addressing the first hypothesis have already been proposed, including the use of drugs that selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells or suppress a wide range of proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors collectively referred to as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Many of these senotherapies have been tested in animal models of cardiovascular disease and aging with promising results.13 From the cardiovascular standpoint, further studies are needed to clarify whether this approach can be as promising as for cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease and whether the use of plasma biomarkers can better predict aging than other validated surrogate biomarkers (e.g. arterial stiffness, calcium score, diastolic dysfunction, pulse wave velocity, and intima–media thickness).14 This study opens a field of exciting future directions of research. Will it be possible to halt or reverse the aging trajectory for a specific organ with lifestyle changes or therapeutic interventions? The idea of having a non-invasive way to address this and related questions is stimulating, and, with the development of more sophisticated computational models, this scenario seems to be within reach. title: The emergence of "Scambling" and regulatory responses to black-market gambling operations
authors: David Norman
abstract: This paper examines the emergence of "scambling" - fraudulent gambling operations that systematically defraud users through sophisticated cybercrime techniques - as a distinct category of transnational financial crime requiring specialised regulatory responses. Through analysis of the Russian-operated Gambler Panel network, which facilitates over 1,200 malicious domains through 20,000 active affiliates, this study investigates how black-market gambling companies exploit regulatory fragmentation to evade local licensing requirements whilst targeting consumers globally. The research explores technical evasion methods including domain hopping, cryptocurrency payment processing, and Content Delivery Network exploitation, alongside regulatory circumvention strategies that exploit jurisdictional differences in enforcement capacity. Key findings reveal that scambling operations achieve industrial scale through "Fraud-as-a-Service" models that democratise criminal capabilities, whilst legitimate gambling operators remain bound by strict withdrawal processing requirements and consumer protection obligations that scambling sites systematically circumvent. The paper argues that the professionalisation of these criminal networks, evidenced by comprehensive operational wikis and franchise-like business models, necessitates enhanced international cooperation, adaptive regulatory frameworks, and recognition of scambling as a distinct threat category requiring coordinated cross-border enforcement responses. The study concludes that whilst current regulatory approaches demonstrate potential effectiveness through initiatives such as URL takedowns and payment provider disruption, the rapid evolution of scambling operations demands increasingly proactive and technologically sophisticated countermeasures to protect consumers and maintain market integrity in the digital gambling ecosystem.Keywords: scambling, online gambling fraud, regulatory evasion, international compliance, cybercrime-as-a-service, cryptocurrency fraud, transnational crime, consumer protection, gambling regulation, black-market operationsIntroductionThe convergence of sophisticated cybercrime techniques with online gambling has given rise to a new category of financial fraud that security researchers have termed "scambling" - a portmanteau of "scam" and "gambling" that describes fraudulent gambling operations designed specifically to defraud users rather than provide legitimate gaming services. Analysis of the August 2025 Krebs on Security investigation reveals a highly organised Russian-operated fraud network known as the Gambler Panel, which has proliferated hundreds of polished online gaming and wagering websites that lure victims with free credits before absconding with any cryptocurrency funds deposited by players (Krebs, 2025). This phenomenon represents not merely an evolution in cybercrime methodology but a fundamental challenge to international gambling regulation, consumer protection frameworks, and cross-border law enforcement cooperation. The scale and sophistication of these operations, combined with their exploitation of regulatory fragmentation across jurisdictions, necessitates a comprehensive examination of how these black-market gambling companies evade local licensing and regulation whilst systematically defrauding consumers globally.Technical architecture of scambling operationsThe Gambler Panel exemplifies the technical sophistication underlying modern scambling operations, functioning as what cybersecurity researchers describe as a "Fraud-as-a-Service" platform that democratises criminal capabilities through franchise-like business models. The platform serves over 1,200 domains through a centralised infrastructure, supporting more than 20,000 active affiliates who promote these fraudulent gambling sites through social media channels including Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube Shorts (Krebs, 2025). The operation's self-described "soulless project that is made for profit" employs what Krebs (2025) reports as a "completely self-written from scratch FAKE CASINO engine" that simulates legitimate gambling experiences whilst ensuring that users can never successfully withdraw funds.The scam follows a predictable pattern: deceptive social media advertisements claim partnerships with popular athletes or social media personalities, offering $2,500 credits through supplied promotional codes. When users attempt to withdraw winnings, the platform rejects requests and demands a "verification deposit" of cryptocurrency, typically around $100, before any money can be distributed (Krebs, 2025). Those who deposit cryptocurrency are subsequently pressed into additional wagering and deposits, with all players eventually losing everything invested in the platform.The technical infrastructure demonstrates remarkable sophistication in evading detection and regulatory oversight. According to cybersecurity research, illegal gambling sites employ Content Delivery Networks such as Cloudflare to obscure origin server IP addresses whilst providing distributed infrastructure that enables rapid domain switching capabilities. This multi-jurisdictional server architecture strategically separates critical infrastructure components across different countries to complicate law enforcement efforts. The Gambler Panel's ability to serve over 1,200 domains from a centralised platform with shared user base, IP tracking, and custom API represents what researchers describe as "a scalable system designed to be a resilient foundation for thousands of disposable scam sites" (Krebs, 2025).International regulatory framework and circumvention methodsThe international online gambling regulatory landscape presents a complex patchwork of jurisdictional approaches that scambling operations systematically exploit. The United Kingdom's Gambling Commission, operating under the Gambling Act 2005, represents one of the world's most comprehensive regulatory frameworks. The Commission reported taking action against 264 unlicensed operators in 2024, removing illegal websites and referring over 102,000 URLs to Google for delisting - (Yogonet, 2025). Despite these efforts, the fragmented nature of international regulation creates numerous opportunities for regulatory arbitrage.Within the European Union, the absence of unified gambling legislation means each member state maintains autonomous regulatory authority, creating a heterogeneous enforcement environment that illegal operators exploit through jurisdictional shopping. The Malta Gaming Authority offers comprehensive licensing with strict requirements for player protection and anti-money laundering compliance, whilst more permissive jurisdictions such as Curacao enable operators to obtain licensing with significantly lower regulatory barriers (Casinos.mt, 2025). This disparity in regulatory standards enables scambling operations to claim legitimacy through association with permissive jurisdictions whilst targeting consumers in strictly regulated markets.The United States operates under a complex federal-state system where individual states regulate within federal constraints established by legislation including the Unlawful Internet Gambling Enforcement Act of 2006. This multi-layered regulatory approach creates enforcement challenges, particularly when illegal operators are based outside US jurisdiction. The scale of regulatory circumvention is substantial, with billions wagered annually with unlicensed operators despite robust legislative frameworks.Regional authority responsibilities and enforcement mechanismsRegional authorities bear primary responsibility for preventing gambling scams within their jurisdictions, yet face significant challenges in enforcing regulations against operations that exist largely outside their territorial control. The UK Gambling Commission has developed one of the most aggressive enforcement stances globally, with dedicated teams focusing on URL takedowns, payment provider disruption, and international regulatory cooperation through organisations such as the International Association of Gaming Regulators.European cooperation efforts involve sixteen EU member states implementing measures requiring payment processors to block transactions with unlicensed operators, though success rates vary significantly based on enforcement resources and political will. The Australian Communications and Media Authority has blocked hundreds of illegal gambling websites, employing Internet Service Provider-level blocking combined with financial institution cooperation to disrupt payment flows to illegal operators.Enforcement mechanisms include both direct and indirect approaches. Direct enforcement tools such as website blocking face limitations from VPN usage and rapid proliferation of mirror sites. Domain seizures, whilst legally powerful, are undermined by operators' ability to establish new domains faster than authorities can process seizures. Criminal prosecution remains the most potent enforcement tool but requires operators to have physical presence or assets within the prosecuting jurisdiction. Indirect enforcement mechanisms, including search engine cooperation and supply chain disruption targeting software providers and advertising platforms, have shown promise in reducing visibility and operational capacity of illegal operators.Withdrawal processing standards and regulatory protectionsOne of the most significant operational differences between legitimate licensed gambling operators and scambling operations lies in withdrawal processing standards and the legal obligations surrounding player fund access. Regulated gambling jurisdictions maintain strict requirements for withdrawal processing times, typically mandating that licensed operators process withdrawal requests within 24 to 72 hours for electronic payments, with many jurisdictions requiring operators to maintain segregated player funds that remain accessible regardless of the operator's financial position (Scams.info, 2025).The UK Gambling Commission's Licence Conditions and Codes of Practice require operators to process withdrawals "without unreasonable delay" and mandate that customer funds be held in separate accounts from operational funds, ensuring player protection even in cases of operator insolvency. Similarly, the Malta Gaming Authority requires licensed operators to process withdrawal requests within five working days for electronic payments, with clear appeal processes for any delays exceeding this timeframe. These regulatory frameworks create enforceable legal obligations that provide players with recourse through regulatory complaints procedures and potential compensation schemes.In contrast, scambling operations deliberately exploit the absence of such protections as a core component of their fraud model. The Gambler Panel's operational manual explicitly instructs affiliates on strategies for delaying and ultimately denying withdrawal requests, including the implementation of "verification deposits" that serve no legitimate security purpose but instead extract additional funds from victims (Krebs, 2025). Unlike licensed operators who face regulatory sanctions, licence revocation, and legal action for failing to process legitimate withdrawals, scambling operations face no legal consequences for withdrawal delays since they operate entirely outside regulatory frameworks.The European Gaming and Betting Association has established industry standards requiring member operators to process at least 95 percent of withdrawal requests within 24 hours, with comprehensive reporting requirements to regulatory authorities for any delays. Licensed operators in jurisdictions such as New Jersey and Pennsylvania must maintain minimum capitalisation requirements and demonstrate sufficient liquidity to meet all outstanding player obligations, providing additional assurance that funds remain available for withdrawal.This fundamental difference in withdrawal obligations represents one of the clearest distinctions between legitimate gambling services and scambling operations, highlighting how regulatory frameworks serve not merely as licensing mechanisms but as essential consumer protection infrastructure that scambling operations systematically circumvent.Consumer protection measures and fraud preventionConsumer protection against scambling operations requires multi-faceted approaches combining regulatory enforcement, consumer education, and technological solutions. The scale of consumer harm is substantial, with global scam losses exceeding $1.03 trillion in 2024, and online gambling fraud experiencing a 64 percent year-over-year increase (Global Anti-Scam Alliance, 2024). The sophistication of scambling operations extends to professional website designs with gaming-quality graphics indistinguishable from legitimate casinos, implementing artificial intelligence to generate convincing testimonials and creating fake app store listings.Warning signs that consumers should recognise include withdrawal restrictions where platforms allow deposits and initial wins but block withdrawals during "security verification," excessive bonuses or guaranteed wins that appear too good to be true, and requests for cryptocurrency payments rather than traditional payment methods. The Gambler Panel's comprehensive wiki provides affiliates with detailed strategies for "fleecing players straight from the playbook," including ready-made templates for social media promotion and scripted responses for customer service interactions (Krebs, 2025).Consumer education initiatives have been developed across multiple jurisdictions to combat scambling operations. The United States Federal Trade Commission's Consumer Sentinel Network provides crucial data for enforcement actions and consumer warnings. The UK's GAMSTOP self-exclusion service represents a proactive approach to protecting vulnerable consumers. Australia's implementation of world-first Scams Prevention Framework legislation in 2025 creates enforceable obligations for businesses across sectors where scammers operate.Recovery options for victims remain limited, with minimal financial recovery rates across all fraud types globally. Financial recovery options include debt management programmes, free nonprofit credit counselling services, and specialised support through organisations such as Gamblers Anonymous. However, victims face additional risks from recovery scams that target those already defrauded, strict reporting deadlines from financial institutions, and jurisdictional complexity that complicates cross-border fund recovery efforts.International cooperation and legal implicationsThe transnational nature of scambling operations necessitates unprecedented levels of international cooperation in regulatory enforcement and law enforcement response. The International Association of Gaming Regulators, comprising 75 jurisdictions, facilitates information sharing and coordinated enforcement actions through its Illegal Gambling Working Group. INTERPOL's Operation SOGA X in 2024 resulted in over 5,100 arrests and $59 million seized across 28 countries, demonstrating the potential effectiveness of coordinated international action.Legal frameworks for addressing scambling operations continue to evolve in response to technological advancement and operational sophistication. World Trade Organization dispute resolution cases have established precedents regarding cross-border gambling services under international trade law, whilst Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties facilitate evidence gathering and information exchange for criminal investigations. However, significant challenges persist in harmonising evidentiary standards across jurisdictions and adapting legal frameworks to address emerging technologies.The role of technology platforms in combating scambling operations has become increasingly critical. Search engines, social media platforms, and app stores serve as key gatekeepers that can significantly impact the visibility and accessibility of fraudulent gambling sites. The UK Gambling Commission's success in removing tens of thousands of URLs from search results demonstrates the potential impact of platform cooperation, yet the rapid proliferation of new domains continues to challenge content moderation systems.Expert perspectives on regulatory challenges "The emergence of 'scambling' operations represents a fundamental evolution in financial crime that exploits the intersection of gambling regulation and cybercrime enforcement. These sophisticated networks operate with the professionalism of legitimate businesses whilst systematically defrauding consumers through regulatory arbitrage and technological sophistication. The Gambler Panel's franchise model demonstrates how criminal enterprises have adopted scalable business practices that require equally sophisticated regulatory responses combining enhanced international cooperation, advanced detection technologies, and adaptive enforcement frameworks." (Norman, 2025)Industry experts emphasise that scambling operations represent not merely a regulatory challenge but a fundamental threat to consumer trust in digital commerce. The sophistication of these operations requires equally sophisticated responses from regulators, law enforcement, and industry stakeholders. The evolution of scambling signals broader trends in cybercrime organisation, particularly the emergence of "Crime-as-a-Service" models that lower barriers to entry for criminal actors whilst creating resilient criminal networks that challenge traditional law enforcement approaches.Future implications and regulatory evolutionSecurity experts predict that scambling operations will continue evolving, incorporating artificial intelligence-powered customer service automation, deepfake technology for celebrity endorsements, and expansion into other fraud categories using similar affiliate models. The integration of emerging technologies such as decentralised hosting solutions, blockchain-based payment systems, and smart contracts for automated gambling operations presents new challenges for regulatory frameworks designed for centralised operators.Regulatory responses must similarly evolve to address these emerging threats. The implementation of machine learning algorithms for pattern recognition, device fingerprinting for multi-account detection, and real-time transaction monitoring represents the technological arms race between fraudsters and regulators. Enhanced collaboration through threat intelligence sharing platforms and integration with law enforcement databases provides the foundation for more effective enforcement.Conclusion: The significance of "Scambling" in regulatory contextsThe emergence of the term "scambling" represents more than linguistic innovation; it signifies recognition within regulatory and cybersecurity communities of a distinct category of criminal enterprise that transcends traditional definitions of either gambling fraud or cyber scams. The term's adoption by authorities including the Australian Consumer and Business Services reflects growing awareness that these operations require specialised regulatory responses addressing both gambling-related components and their fundamental nature as systematic fraud enterprises.The Gambler Panel network, with its 20,000 active affiliates and over 1,200 domains, exemplifies how scambling operations have achieved industrial scale whilst maintaining operational resilience against regulatory countermeasures. The platform's detailed wiki, which provides comprehensive guidance on "fleecing players" and includes ready-made customer service responses and marketing templates, demonstrates the professionalisation of fraud that challenges traditional enforcement approaches (Krebs, 2025).The regulatory significance of scambling extends beyond immediate consumer protection concerns to fundamental questions about the adequacy of existing international legal frameworks for addressing transnational digital crime. The exploitation of regulatory fragmentation, jurisdictional limitations, and technological innovation by scambling operations highlights systemic vulnerabilities in global gambling regulation that require coordinated international response.Ultimately, the scambling phenomenon represents a convergence of technological capability, criminal innovation, and regulatory challenge that demands comprehensive response across multiple domains. The integration of enhanced international cooperation, advanced detection technologies, robust consumer education, and adaptive regulatory frameworks provides the foundation for effective response. However, the rapid evolution of scambling operations and their demonstrated ability to exploit emerging technologies suggests that regulatory authorities must adopt increasingly proactive and innovative approaches to protect consumers from these sophisticated fraud enterprises. The term "scambling" thus serves not merely as description but as a call to action for regulators, law enforcement, and industry stakeholders to recognise and respond to this evolving threat to consumer protection and market integrity in the digital age.References Casinos.MT (2025) 'International Gambling License Comparison', Casinos.MT MGA licensing directory and information, 30 September 2025. title: Artificial Intelligence for Multiple Long-term conditions (AIM): A consensus statement from the NIHR AIM consortia
authors: Hajira Dambha‐Miller; Andrew A. Farmer; Krishnarajah Nirantharakumar; Thomas Jackson; Christopher Yau; Lauren Elizabeth Walker et al.
abstract: Artificial Intelligence for Multiple Long-term conditions (AIM): A consensus statement from the NIHR AIM consortia Hajira Dambha-Miller1, Andrew Farmer2, Krishnarajah Nirantharakumar3, Thomas Jackson4 Christopher Yau5,6,7, Lauren Walker8 Iain Buchan9, Sarah Finer10, Michael R Barnes10, Nick J Reynolds11, Gyuchan Thomas Jun12, Satheesh Gangadharan13, Simon Fraser 14 and Bruce Guthrie8 Primary Care Research Centre, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK. Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK. Institute of Applied Health Research, University of Birmingham Institute of Inflammation and Ageing, University of Birmingham Nuffield Department of Women's & Reproductive Health, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK Nuffield Department of Population Health, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK Health Data Research, London, UK Institute of Systems, Molecular and Integrative Biology, University of Liverpool, Liverpool, UK Institute of Population Health, University of Liverpool, Liverpool, UK Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry, Queen Mary University of London, London, UK Institute of Translational and Clinical Medicine, Newcastle University Medical School, Newcastle upon Tyne, UK School of Design and Creative Arts, Loughborough University, UK Leicestershire Partnership NHS Trust, UK Department of Public Health, University of Southampton Usher Institute, University of Edinburgh Correspondence: Dr Hajira Dambha-Miller, Primary Care Research Centre, University of Southampton, Southampton, SO16 5ST, Email: H.Dambha-Miller@soton.ac.uk Abstract Recent advances in causal machine learning and wider artificial intelligence (AI) methods could provide new insights into the natural histories and potential prevention of clusters of multiple long-term conditions or multimorbidity (MLTC-M). When combined with expertise in clinical practice, applied health research and social science, there is potential to systematically identify and map new clusters of disease, understand the trajectories of patients with these conditions throughout their life course, predict serious adverse outcomes, optimise therapies and consider the influence of wider determinants such as environmental, behavioural and psychosocial factors. The National Institute of Health Research (NIHR) recently funded multidisciplinary consortia to bring together AI specialists, experts in big data and MLTC-M in the first and second waves of this new programme. The so-called AIM consortia of researchers will spearhead the use of artificial intelligence methods and develop insights for the identification and subsequent prevention of MLTC-M. This consensus agreement is aimed at facilitating a community of learning within the AIM consortia, promoting cooperation, transparency and rigour in our approaches while maintaining high methodological standards and consistency in defining and reporting within our research. In bringing together these research collaborations, there is also an opportunity to foster shared learning, synergies and rapidly compare and validate new AI approaches across our respective studies. This step is critical to implementation on the pathway to patient and public benefit. Scope and aim This statement was developed by the first and second wave of the NIHR AIM consortia and includes representatives across thirteen universities from Edinburgh, Birmingham, Oxford, Southampton, Nottingham, Kent, Manchester, St. Andrews, Liverpool, Newcastle, QMUL, Loughborough and UCL. The multidisciplinary collaborations include front-line primary, secondary and social care staff; researchers in primary, secondary, and social care; health informatics and data science (including AI) experts; epidemiologists; qualitative researchers; statisticians; clinical and health services researchers, geographers; health economists; sociologists, human factors design researchers and public contributors. A summary of each study represented within the AIM consortia and their respective aims is included below. The agreements reached are entirely those of the consortia; sponsors and funders have had no role in the development or reporting of this statement. After initial discussions on the need for such a statement in our individual projects, we met to refine ideas and reach an agreement on item inclusion. We acknowledged variations in aims and purpose of research but found shared interest and overlapping aims with regards to the development of MLTC-M clusters that could then be externally validated across our respective studies. We collectively agreed on the need for a priori consensus on definitions of MLTC-M, clustering variables, outcomes, managing data requests, as well transparency in reporting and methodological approaches to permit meaningful comparison between findings and validation that in turn, could contribute toward more rapid translation to patient benefit. Summary of studies included within wave 1 and 2 of the AIM consortia The development and validation of population clusters for integrating health and social care: A mixed-methods study on Multiple Long-Term Conditions (AIM-Cluster) Principal Investigators: Hajira Dambha-Miller and Andrew Farmer Aim: To develop and validate population clusters that consider health and social care determinants and subsequent need for people with MLTC-M using data-driven AI methods compared to expert-driven approaches, followed by evaluation of cluster trajectories and their association with health outcomes and costs. Study Design: AI methods, Delph and Qualitative: Semi-automated based on shallow machine learning clustering using expert crafted features calculated from raw data; Fully-automated based on deep artificial neural networks and explainable AI techniques Databases: CRPD Aurum and Gold, SAIL, ELSA Follow up: 10 years Outcomes: For each cluster; Development of additional MLTC-M, All-cause mortality, Cause-mortality, Worsening frailty, Health and social care costs OPTIMising therapies, disease trajectories and AI-assisted clinical management for patients Living with complex multimorbidity (OPTIMAL study) Principal Investigators; Thomas Jackson and Krishnarajah Nirantharakumar Aim: To integrate multimodal primary care, secondary care, qualitative, and prescribing data to develop an AI tool with the aim of optimising clinical decision making in patients with cMM. Study Design: AI methods and Mixed method Databases: CPRD Aurum/GOLD, PIONEER, INSIGHT, Scottish data (Linked Tayside and Fife Database and Greater Glasgow and Clyde) Follow-up: Up to 10 years Outcomes: Trajectories of distinct phenotypes in clusters and time-points for prevention, Predictive algorithms for future morbidities, Predictive algorithm for choice of medication in the context of multimorbidity, Discovery of medications for repurposing Artificial Intelligence and Multimorbidity: Clustering in Individuals, Space and Clinical Context (AIM-CISC) Principal Investigators; Bruce Guthrie Aim: To use artificial intelligence and state-of-the-art data science, social science and health service research methods to understand clustering of morbidities within individuals, within communities, and in key clinical contexts. Study Design: AI methods and Mixed methods Databases: : CPRD Aurum, Lothian DataLoch, UK Biobank, Generation Scotland, Scottish Longitudinal Study, Lothian Data Follow-up: Up to 10 years Outcomes: Objective 1: morbidity clusters, Objective 2: morbidity clusters from objective 1, Objective 3: morbidity clusters from objective 1 and a priori multimorbidty groups, Objective 4: serious adverse events of various kinds (eg delirium, falls, increasing dependency, hospital admission, care home admission, death). DynAIRx: AIs for dynamic prescribing optimisation and care integration in multimorbidity (DynAIRx) Principal Investigators; Lauren Walker and Iain Buchan Aim: To extract information from scattered clinical records on how health and medication change over time, apply AI and statistical approaches to predict risk of poor outcomes and develop visualisations that overlay these combined data to enable easier review of medications. We shall pilot this approach in GP prescribing audit and feedback systems, and co-design future medicines optimisation decision support systems with patients and prescribers. Study Design : AI methods and qualitative engagement Databases: Structured data from care records across Cheshire & Merseyside, Greater Manchester, and Yorkshire & Humber, covering a population of ~11m using the www.cipha.nhs.uk blueprint that links population health management with care workflow, so can provide data for AI test/train and feedback actionable information to prescribers. Follow-up: Up to 12 years Outcomes: Patterns and clusters of conditions, medications, tests and clinical contacts preceding adverse events identified by AI in key high-risk groups (older people with frailty; coexisting physical and mental health problems; complex multimorbidity and problematic polypharmacy). Build the patterns into biostatistical causal inference and prediction of (clustered) clinical outcomes, Advance visualisation of longitudinal summaries of multi-provider care records overlain combined with key features from AI-learned patterns/structures, AI-augmented multimorbidity information built into an existing prescribing audit and feedback system – creating a learning system for medicines optimisation AI-Multiply - Using artificial intelligence (AI) to characterize the dynamic inter-relationships between MUltiple Long-term condiTIons and PoLYpharmacy and across diverse UK populations and inform health care pathways (AI-Multiply) Principal Investigators; Nick Reynolds and Michael Barnes Aim: To characterise MLTC-M and polypharmacy (MLTC-M-PP) trajectories and define the interrelationships between MLTC-M clusters, polypharmacy, inequalities and healthcare outcomes over the life course Study Design: AI methods and mixed methods Databases: Follow-up: Up to 10 years Outcomes: Polypharmacy, All-cause mortality, Premature mortality,Healthcare utilisation, MLTC-M inflection point trial emulation Interdisciplinary, theory-informed guidance, A defined and operational PPI strategy influencing study outcomes.Refined pipelines of data engineering, AI and ML methodology. Defined MLTC-M-PP clusters, replicated cross-methods and cross-data sets. External validation of MLTC-M-PP clusters.Defined drivers of MLTC-M-PP clusters including influence of intersectional factors.Theoretically informed guidance for future AI-in-health collaborations, based on interdisciplinary understanding of ideas, assumptions and knowledge creation. New interventions to improve long-term treatment of patients, for testing in pragmatic trials.Identification of a partner to develop MLTC-M-PP clinical decision support tools and identification of potential 'tipping’ points. Enhanced training of early career researchers and increased critical mass in interdisciplinary MLTC research. Data-driven machine-learning aided stratification and management of multiple long-term conditions in adults with intellectual disabilities (DECODE) Principal Investigators; Gyuchan Thomas Jun and Satheesh Gangadharan Aim: To apply machine learning approaches to identify clusters and trajectories of MLTCs in people with intellectual disabilities and to utilise them to develop actionable insights for effective care coordination to improve the health and wellbeing of people with intellectual disabilities Study Design: AI methods and mixed methods Databases: Follow-up: Up to 20 years Outcomes: New knowledge on clusters and trajectories of MLTCs and a model of effective care coordination for people with intellectual disabilities Multidisciplinary Ecosystem to study Lifecourse Determinants and Prevention of Early-onset Burdensome Multimorbidity (MELD-B) Principal Investigators; Simon Fraser and Nisreen Alwan Aim: To safely deliver an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced epidemiological analytic system in which optimal lifecourse time points and targets for prevention of early-onset, burdensome multimorbidity are identified through multidisciplinary synthesis and analysis of birth cohorts and electronic health records, and disseminated to key stakeholders Study Design: AI methods and mixed methods Databases: Follow-up: Birth to age 65 for the primary analyses Outcomes: A suite of burdensomeness/complexity indicators. Novel, burdensome MLTC-M clusters, Summary of early-life and wider determinants of burdensome cluster, Summary of critical time points and targets for intervention, Models of potential ‘preventable moments’ of early, burdensome MLTC-M.Co-produced public health implementation recommendations. Defining MLTC-M Researchers acknowledged the substantial variations within the literature in defining MLTC-M and in the conditions that might be included under this terminology.[1] [2]Moreover, each consortium may have a slightly different clinical or public health focus meriting inclusion of a diverse range of conditions [ref]. Acknowledging these challenges, the consortia agreed to conform to the definition of MLTC-M set out by Guthrie et al., (paper in submission) and to include a minimum set of conditions within our data requests based on the 59 core conditions summarised in figure 1 below. Not all these conditions will be relevant to every study and indeed researchers will include additional conditions. However, agreement on the availability of a minimum set of conditions by every consortium will facilitate future external validation across studies. will include within data requests and approvals, opportunities for unspecified replication for other studies within the NIHR AIM programme of research[3]. This is an essential step to achieving the overall objective of cross-collaboration replication and validation. Code-sets and analytical code should also be made available. We constructed clinical code lists using a rigorous process, which involved reviewing existing code lists (e.g., CALIBER and Cambridge CPRD codes), applying comprehensive search terms to identify codes and finally review by clinicians and where necessary a consensus process to produce the final list of codes. The process is documented for transparency and was developed using the DExtER code builder. Initial code list was generated by the University of Birmingham for the 59 agreed conditions and shared freely across the consortia. Individual groups will include additional codes where appropriate according to their projects. Analytical code will be [4,5]available through the HDR-UK phenotype library. title: Editorial: Neurobiological foundations of cognition and progress toward artificial general intelligence
authors: Yufik Yan; Robert Kozma; James Kroger
abstract: The problems are as follows: a) what is intelligence, b) how human intelligence differs from that in the other species, c) how could intelligence emerge in the physical universe, d) what is the future of AI? e) The last decade has witnessed breakthrough advances in machine learning methods rooted in the ideas of digital neurons and perceptron dating back to the mid 20 th century, what factors have been responsible for these advances? To facilitate discussion, we outline opinions and hypothetical solutions that are intended as discussion starters and encompass theoretical foundations, synopsis of contributions in this volume and a new synthesis.First, the opinions. a) According to a definition attributed to Jean Piaget "intelligence is what you use when you don't know what to do, when neither innateness nor learning has prepared you for the particular situation" (Calvin, 1996, p.1)) Novel situations engage the understanding capacity in a dual function of constructing adequate responses and overcoming the inertia of prior learning (the legacy mind set) interfering with the construction. b) All species are capable of learning while the understanding capacity is uniquely human. c) Intelligence mechanisms are hypothesized to be integral to those underlying the emergence of life and involving self-organization in networks of interacting elements where parts of networks fold into stable units separated by an active surface ("membrane") from their surrounds (Friston, 2010). d) The future of AI involves transition from machine learning to machine understanding centered on the approximation of meaning creation in self-organizing neuronal networks. e) Machine learning methods are computationally demanding. Their successes have been due to a confluence of two developments: ingenious heuristics to minimize computational demands and a trillion-fold increase of hardware efficiency. Machine understanding will employ moderate capacity platforms with low energy demands to deliver functions inaccessible to learning (Yufik et al, 2026). Next, the hypotheses.1. The foundations.In the history of psychology, behaviorism was reducing intelligence to conditioning while cognitivism has been equating intelligence to computation. The "Bayesian intelligence" school of thought conceptualizes brain as a "prediction machine". Theories of understanding conceptualize human brain as a biophysical system for the production of meaning and pivot on the ideas of "neuronal packets" and "wave packets" (Yufik et al, 2026;Yufik 1998;Freeman, 2000;Kozma et al, 2026). The former idea coheres with the key insight in Gestalt psychology: "Sensory units have acquired names, have become symbolic and known to have practical uses while they have existed as units before any of these further facts were added. … it is precisely the original segregation of circumscribed wholes which makes it possible for the sensory world to appear so utterly imbued with meaning" (Kohler, 1947, p.82) The "wave packets" idea attributes production of meaning to amplitude-and phase-modulated waves of activity percolating through systems of interacting neuronal populations. Suggestions for the integration of the two conceptions are stated in Section 3.Understanding involves "apprehending general relations in multitudes of particulars" (Webster's Dictionary). A parable of blind men and an elephant comes in handy: meaning is produced in constructing relations that integrate disparate reports into a coherent whole (assume a blind analyst charged with the task). Integration enables explanation and prediction: elephants behave differently from any of the entities in the reports. Piaget's theory characterizes understanding as "the system of operational co-ordinations that transform objects of thought in the same way as actions transform material objects… in order to understand, one must be able to construct in thought indefinite series … and treat the series one has actually observed as just one sector of an unlimited range of possibilities" (Piaget 1978, p. 222).Another critical insight in psychology concerns the dynamics of (the "movement of consciousness" in) coordinating some object Z with other objects, starting will accessing Z: "Through hovering of the attention in the neighborhood of the desired object, the accumulation of associates becomes so great that the combined tension of their neural processes break through the bar, and the nervous wave pours into the tract which has so long been awaiting its advent…The activities in Z will at first be a mere tension …until combined irradiations upon Z succeed in helping the tension there to overcome the resistance and is arousing Z to full activity" (James, 1950, v.1, p. 586).Finally, the most fundamental, cornerstone idea in psychology and neuroscience is the idea of neuronal assemblies by Donald Hebb, conceptualizing groups of neurons as the basic functional units in the neuronal system. A critical insight concerns interaction between assembles in the formation of percepts (e.g. assemblies a, b, c interact in forming the percept of triangle ABC):"…simultaneous activity in a, b, c would establish facilitation between them, through their chance anatomical interconnections and the enlargement of synaptic knobs… The resulting superordinate system must be essentially a new one, by no means a sum of hooking together of a, b and c…a better notation for the new structure is t: the assembly of cells whose activity…is perception of the triangle as a distinctive whole" Hebb, 1947, p. 97) In the emerging integrated picture so far, bringing together in imagination two "segregated wholes" appears to be one of the basic operations in meaning creation. Unsurprisingly, a received theory of language understanding places operation Merge (combining some objects Z and some X into a unit) at the core of the capacity (Chomsky 2004(Chomsky , 2014;;Berwick, 2016). We will return to these notions in Section 3, after re-centering the discussion as follows.Production of meaning is coextensive with making choices (which Z, which X?): automatisms admit no choices, choices are drilled in from the outside in learning and are decided internally in understanding. An array of 10 objects affords 1,024 choices, accounting for permutations (A after B is not the same as B after A) increases that number to 3, 628, 800. Boundary barriers (or "bars" James, 1950, v.1, p. 586) turn culling through combinations into steeplechase running, multiple objects (e.g. 32 chess pieces) yield astronomically large combinatorial spaces: how can the human system run steeplechase marathons and real time sprints in such spaces while subsisting on miniscule energy budgets? "Operational coordination" (Piaget 1978, p. 222) transforms combinations into coherent structures (models) amenable to coordination with other models: what mechanisms drive the expanding coherence? Section 3 ventures a hypothesis: understanding compresses combinatorial spaces into minute volumes imbued with meaning. Section 2 highlights connections between the articles in this volume, the questions above and the theory in Section 3.Davis, Shuebeler and Kirk https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/systems-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnsys.2025.1718733/full analyze EEG data to assess the degree of coherence in neuronal processes, on the assumption that high coherence corresponds to achieving mental clarity and entering into a meditative state of mind. Following the Global Workspace Theory, the paper attributes achieving coherence to global information broadcasting and active integration, with the spotlight of consciousness illuminating the salient contents. Conscious awareness can also include "silent" elements having no reportable sensory content . Global coherence is equated to synchronization entailing reduction of entropy. Dodig -Crnkovich https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/systemsneuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnsys.2026.1730097/full presents a broadly conceptualized analysis of biological cognition and AI, addressing the possible origins and observable manifestation of intelligence in the physical universe. Within this all-encompassing framework (Info-Computational Framework, or ICON) the mind is viewed as a material phenomenon in a continuum stretching from inanimate substances to primitive organisms and up to sentient beings. The article includes definitions of general notions, e.g. "information is a difference that makes a difference for the regulation of system environment interactions", etc. The intended meaning of such definitions is explicated in the analysis, including validation approaches.Wright, David and Bourke https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/systems-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnsys.2025.1683448/full offer an elegant interpretation of embryogenesis dynamics in terms of predictive error minimization. The predictive error minimization framework is given a dual application: an explanatory principle in a theory of selforganization dynamics in the embryo and a mathematical tool for predicting that dynamics from data (embryo viability, etc.) The proposed theory views synaptically linked neurons as coupled oscillators, self-organization drives synaptic fluxes towards equilibrium in a synchronized state where each couple functions as an element in Markov blanket that maintains equilibrium in the system and causes convergence towards error minimization.Vavrecka and Wermter https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/systems-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnsys.2025.1683133/full argue that Large Language Models (LLN) fail to address the symbol grounding problem and operate strictly on the basis of statistical regularities. They contend that closing conceptual gaps between symbolic tokens, neural representations, and embodied experiences will require a theoretical framework accounting for the integration of continuous sensory flows, goal-directed behavior and neural learning.Grossberg https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/systems-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnsys.2025.1630151/full reviews developments in Adaptive Resonance Theory (ART) since the time of its inception and presents new results, comparing performance in ART to that in LLM. The article argues that progress towards AGI will lead to Autonomous Adaptive Intelligence (AAI) systems implementing the core ART intuition: learning proceeds in an interplay between bottom-up and top-down processes. Comparing AAI to LLM highlights the limitations of the latter rooted in the limitations of deep learning.Kirkpatrick https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/systems-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnsys.2025.1695493/full argues insightfully that human intelligence is fundamentally grounded in motion and asserts that AGI will thoroughly integrate motion and cognition and thus escape from the circular logic inherent in the computational metaphor. A critical limitation of such models is manifested in their ability to emulate proofs of mathematical propositions but not the processes that underlie the understanding of those proofs. The paper makes constructive suggestions for the development of biologically inspired AGI.Rachman and Pashea https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sociology/articles/10.3389/fsoc.2026.1646503/full associate human intelligence with problem solving in diverse contexts under a general objective of minimizing uncertainty. title: An unexpected fall from GRACE
authors: Daniela Pedicino; Giovanna Liuzzo
abstract: Comment on ‘Effectiveness of GRACE risk score in patients admitted to hospital with non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome (UKGRIS): parallel group cluster randomised controlled trial’ which was published in the British Medical Journal, https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2022-073843. The UK GRACE Risk Score Intervention Study (UKGRIS) is a multicentre, parallel-group, cluster-randomised, registry-based, controlled trial aimed at assessing the effectiveness of risk stratification through the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) risk score (GRS) for patients with suspected non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) on hospital admission.1 A total of 42 hospitals participating in the UK national heart attack registry were randomised 1:1 to standard care or GRS-stratification-guided management. The study recruited 3050 participants in 38 eligible clusters (20 GRS, n = 1440 patients; 18 standard care, n = 1610 patients). The mean age ± standard deviation (SD) was 66 ± 12 years (69% males, 90% Whites), with a mean baseline GRACE score of 119.5 ± 31.4 in the standard care group and 125.7 ± 34.4 in the GRS group. Overall, 67% of patients had non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), 13% had unstable angina, and 20% had a final diagnosis different from NSTE-ACS. Primary outcomes were the use of class I guideline-recommended treatments and time to the composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, new onset heart failure hospitalisation, and readmission for cardiovascular events over 12-month follow-up. Secondary endpoints included the duration of hospital stay, EQ-5D-5L (five-domain, five-level version of the EuroQoL index), and the composite endpoint components. The assignment to GRS did not significantly increase the rate of uptake of guideline-recommended care processes compared with standard care [77.3% for GRS and 75.3% for standard care, odds ratio (OR) 1.16; 95% confidence interval (CI), .70 to 1.92; P = .56]. The 12-month composite cardiac event rates were 34% for GRS and 36.2% for standard care [hazard ratio (HR), .89; 95% CI .68 to 1.16; P = .37]. Baseline adjusted EQ-5D-5L utility (difference −.01; 95% CI −.06 to .04) and the duration of hospital stay (mean 11.2 ± 18 vs. 11.8 ± 19 days) were similar in the two groups. Non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) represents one of the leading causes of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with a high economic burden. Guideline-directed management might significantly improve prognosis, being associated with greater survival gains among those with higher baseline risk.2,3 Prior research has shown that clinical assessment of patient risk is inferior to objective risk tools, thus several prognostic models have been developed to estimate the future risk of adverse events. Among the scores available in this setting, the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) risk score (GRS) offers the best discriminative performance.4,5 The model includes eight variables for risk prediction (age, systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, serum creatinine, cardiac arrest at admission, elevated cardiac biomarkers, ST-segment deviation, and the Killip class at presentation), with good discrimination between low- and high-risk patients and good prognostic value.6 The use of the GRS is recommended in NSTE-ACS management according to international guidelines, with early invasive revascularisation strategy indicated as a class I recommendation for patients with a score >140.2 However, this recommendation lacks supportive evidence, with limited applicability in clinical practice. A previous trial, the Australian GRACE Risk score Intervention Study (AGRIS), randomised patients with ACS to GRS use vs. usual care.7 The trial was stopped early because it failed demonstrating any additive value with the implementation of the GRS in routine clinical practice. This was, at least in part, explained by the high performance of the control hospitals, and by the presence of patients with STEMI in the study population, who routinely receive emergency coronary angiography and associated therapies. The UK GRACE Risk Score Intervention Study study is, together with the AGRIS, the first randomised trial investigating the impact of the utilization of GRS on adherence to guidelines and outcomes.1 Differently from the AGRIS, only NSTE-ACS patients were included at the time of hospital admission. As stated by the authors, the inconclusive results might have been affected by: (i) the higher standards of the control group, resulting in optimal drug treatment in both arms of the trial; (ii) the lower rate of coronary angiography performed at 24 h (12%) and 72 h (54%) among those eligible to receive these care processes, which may suggest non-compliance with GRS recommendations in some centres; and (iii) the use of electronic health records, which is associated with possible misclassification of events. Furthermore, the study was underpowered to detect a modest effect size, and it should also be considered that, despite the same clinical presentation and treatment, NSTE-ACS include a broad spectrum of conditions, with different features of instability underlying a common symptom. In this scenario, the indication on how to deal with patients who are deemed at high or low risk according to GRS is still uncertain. Increasing evidence suggests indeed that different unstable plaques might deserve different management, and filling this gap might help achieving a better risk assessment and implementing effective targeted treatments.8–10 In conclusion, in line with previous evidence, this trial shows that GRS use is not associated with improved adherence to guideline-directed management of NSTE-ACS or reduced cardiovascular events at 12 months compared with standard care. In the era of machine learning and digital advances, further studies will probably clarify how to refine existing models to guide decision-making in the setting of acute coronary syndromes.11 Supplementary data are not available at European Heart Journal online.
