There is an inverse relationship between infectious diseases and immune pathologies. From Bach (2002). Early and late-acting influences on the immune system may underpin the Hygiene Hypothesis. Maternal infection status, breastfeeding, and mode of delivery may promote tolerance in the infant. Changes in diet at weaning and the use of antibiotics in infancy alter the microbiome with lifelong impacts on the risk of obesity, allergies, and autoimmune diseases. After Maizels (2020). Pathways of allergic inflammation and helminth immune modulation. Helminths penetrate and damage epithelial tissue, releasing parasite PAMPs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns) and host DAMPs (damage-associated molecular patterns), which induce type 2 inflammation (colored red) and antigen presentation by dendritic cells (DCs) that generate type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2) and helper T cells (Th2). ILC2 cells in turn induce eosinophils and IgE from B cells, which mediate allergy. If the helminth is immunomodulatory, a regulatory network is invoked (colored green), and DCs may instead induce regulatory T cells (Tregs) that produce suppressive cytokines (interleukin (IL)-10 and transforming growth factor (TGF)-ß). These act on B cells to switch to IgG4 production, on macrophages to assume an anti-inflammatory (M2) phenotype, and on effector Th2 cells to block activation and develop tolerance. By inhibiting both helminth-specific and bystander (e.g. allergen-specific) reactivity, they create a profound anti-inflammatory effect (Maizels 2020). Ig: immunoglobulin. A system’s state can be analyzed as a time series, where change in the values of a state variable of interest are plotted as a function of time (a). Alternatively, two or more state variables can be plotted against each other in a phase portrait (b). Changes in a system’s state trace a trajectory that gives a visual representation of the system’s behavior. In response to perturbation, systems that are in stable equilibrium return to the equilibrium state, while unstable systems deviate further from equilibrium state (a). A stable equilibrium state is called the attractor state. The maximum deviation from the attractor state that a system can recover from is known as the basin of attraction (b). Attractors can be weak or strong, depending on how easy or hard it is to push the system away from the stable state (c). Robustness and resilience are characteristics of attractors defined by the strength of the attractor and the size of the basin of attraction. Interactions among a system’s components. In negative feedback (a), the effect of x on y is positive and effect of y on x is negative. Negative feedback results in a system’s stability. In positive feedback (b) the effects of x and y on each other have the same sign—either both positive or both negative. Positive feedbacks make a system unstable and can drive it to a different state. In feedforward loops (c), the effects of the components move in one direction. The sign of the effects can be positive, negative, or a combination. One use of feedforward loops is to adapt the system to new conditions. A homeostatic circuit. Here, x is a value of a homeostatic variable, x' is the set point value, and |x – x'| is the absolute deviation of x from x'. The sensor detects the value of x and compares it to x'. If x is not equal to x', the sensor generates a signal that acts on the effector. The effector then changes the value of x to reduce its deviation from the set point x'. A rheostatic circuit. The sensor detects the change in a state variable (?x) and produces a signal that promotes adaptation of the target organs to the new value of x. The affected target organs are referred to as ‘affectors’ to distinguish them from the ‘effectors’ of homeostasis. Rheostatic circuits use feedforward control, unlike homeostatic circuits, which are based on negative feedback control. Homeostatic and rheostatic circuits often operate together. A sensor detects the change in a state variable (?x) and produces a signal that promotes homeostasis when it acts on effectors, and adaptation when it acts on affectors. Conformity and regulation are two strategies of dealing with changes in environmental conditions. In conformers, internal state changes to conform with the environmental condition. Regulators maintain the internal state in the face of environmental changes. Regulators are able to maintain stability within a narrow range of environmental conditions, whereas conformers can survive extreme conditions, but at the cost of other physiological functions, including growth and reproduction. title: Novel Insights Into the Spread of Enteric Pathogens Using Genomics
authors: Daryl Domman; Christopher Ruis; Matthew J. Dorman; Migun Shakya; Patrick Chain
abstract: Diarrheal diseases continue to be a leading cause of mortality and morbidity across the globe. The use of next-generation sequencing data has provided major insights into understanding epidemiological spread, antimicrobial resistance, vaccine effects, and basic mechanisms of bacterial and viral evolution. Here, we discuss how genomic data have informed investigations across enteric pathogens, such as Shigella, Vibrio cholerae, Salmonella Typhi, rotavirus, and norovirus. Diarrhea remains one of the leading causes of death globally, with an estimated 1.6 million deaths per year across all ages [1]. In children aged <5 years, diarrhea is the fourth leading cause of death, with an estimated 446 000 deaths per year [1]. In addition to the devastating mortality caused by diarrhea, there are substantial losses, especially for children, in growth and development [2]. The 2016 estimate of the impact of diarrhea was 40 125 700 disability-adjusted life-years in all children aged <5 years [2]. While over the past 25 years there has been a steady decline in deaths due to diarrhea across all ages, with a decrease of 56% of deaths among children younger than 5 years [1], diarrheal disease continues to be leading cause of mortality and morbidity across all age groups (Figure 1). Estimated number of deaths due to enteric pathogens from 1990 to 2017. Data are from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017 (available at: http://ghdx.healthdata.org/gbd-results-tool). E. coli, Escherichia coli; S. Paratyphi, Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphi; S. Typhi, Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar Typhi. Two major efforts have provided estimates of the etiologies of diarrheal diseases across multiple sites. The Global Enteric Multicenter Study (GEMS) was a 3-year, prospective, case-control study across 7 sites across Africa and Asia that aimed to identify the etiologies of pediatric diarrheal diseases [3]. This study highlighted that rotavirus, Cryptosporidium, Shigella, and heat-stable toxin–producing enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ST-ETEC) accounted for the majority of moderate-to-severe diarrhea cases [3]. A subsequent reanalysis of GEMS samples, using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), led to revised estimates that 78% of diarrhea cases were contributed (in descending order) by Shigella, rotavirus, adenovirus 40/41, ST-ETEC, Cryptosporidium, and Campylobacter [4]. Similarly, the Etiology, Risk Factors, and Interactions of Enteric Infections and Malnutrition and the Consequences for Child Health and Development Project (MAL-ED) was a multisite birth cohort study across 8 sites in South America, Africa, and Asia aiming to estimate etiologies of all diarrhea in children aged <2 years [5]. MAL-ED differs from GEMS in that the former relied on intense community surveillance for diarrhea cases, included cases of all severity types (not just moderate-to-severe cases), and examined the pathogen burden in stool specimens from children without diarrhea. MAL-ED found that, during the first year of life, the pathogens of most importance were (in decreasing order of importance), norovirus GII, rotavirus and Campylobacter, astrovirus, and Cryptosporidium. Among individuals in the second year of life, they found that Campylobacter, norovirus GII, rotavirus, astrovirus, and Shigella accounted for the most important fractions [5]. Given the tremendous burden of disease caused by diarrheal illness, the use of molecular and genomic approaches has recently shed much insight on these pathogens. The advent of next-generation sequencing has had tremendous impact on our understanding of nearly every facet of enteric pathogens, including the epidemiological characteristics of global spread, the tracking of antimicrobial resistance, the effects of vaccination, and the basic mechanisms of bacterial and viral evolution. Here, we give a high-level overview of how next-generation sequencing has increased our understanding of bacterial and viral enteric pathogens. Shigellosis is caused by members of the bacterial genus Shigella and was the second leading cause of mortality due to diarrheal disease in 2016, with an estimated 212 400 deaths (Figure 1) [6]. Shigellosis presents initially as fever, headache, and vomiting, followed hours later by watery diarrhea [7]. While most shigellosis cases present with mild symptoms, in some cases there is a progression to frank dysentery associated with frequent stools containing blood and mucus [7]. Microbiologically, Shigella species are gram-negative, nonmotile rods that are members of the bacterial family Enterobacteriaceae. While Shigella species are phylogenetically part of the E. coli complex with multiple origins therein, for historical, clinical, and epidemiological purposes the Shigella genus designation has been retained [8, 9]. It may be that, in the future, Shigella are reclassified as E. coli pathovars and a new nomenclature is adopted by consensus, similar to what occurred for the Salmonella taxonomy [10]. All Shigella species harbor a large virulence plasmid that is essential to host invasion [11]. There are 4 major species of Shigella responsible for infection in humans: S. flexneri, S. sonnei, S. dysenteriae, and S. boydii. Shigella species typically spread from person to person via the fecal oral route, which is facilitated by its low infectious dose. As few as 10 colony-forming units (CFUs) of S. dysenteriae type 1, and nearly 200 CFUs for S. flexneri or S. sonnei can lead to an infection [7]. In low- and middle-income settings, S. flexneri is the leading cause of shigellosis. S. sonnei is the second leading cause of shigellosis in low- and middle-income settings and the leading cause in high-income settings. An interesting switch in the burden of disease from S. flexneri to S. sonnei is often seen in economies transitioning from low to middle income. S. dysenteriae serotype 1 is responsible for pandemic dysentery, which is associated with large-scale outbreaks with high case-fatality rates. S. boydii appears to be rather restricted in geographical spread to Bangladesh and Southeast Asia [12]. The prevalence of S. dysenteriae and S. boydii within the GEMS was 5.0% and 5.4%, respectively, across 1130 Shigella isolates [13]. S. flexneri is the leading cause of endemic shigellosis in low- and middle-income settings, accounting for nearly 75% of shigellosis cases [7]. There are currently 19 serotypes of S. flexneri, based serologically on the major type-specific somatic antigen (I–VI) and common group factor antigens (3, 4, 6, 7, and 8) [14], with the majority of disease due to serotypes 2a, 2b, 3a, and 6 [13]. While serotyping has been the dominant language used to describe how stains are transmitting, early genetic studies indicated that serotypes were not monophyletic [15]. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has lent much insight into proving a clear picture of the natural history and transmission of S. flexneri. To date, the largest study, by Connor et al [16], compared 351 isolates collected during 1913–2011 from 37 countries and yielded the most complete picture of the temporal and geographic spread of this pathogen. This study showed that the population structure of S. flexneri is divided into 7 lineages or phylogenetic groups. Multiple serotypes were found within and across all phylogenetic groups, indicating that serotyping is not a reliable marker for relatedness of strains. The population structure of S. flexneri indicates that lineages have persisted in regions for long periods (the most recent common ancestor [MRCA] for lineages was estimated to have been present between the 1300s and the mid-1800s) [8], with limited intercontinental transmission, a striking difference from the recent intercontinental spread of S. sonnei [17]. While S. flexneri strains have increasingly acquired antimicrobial resistance genes over time, these acquisitions have not led to the lineage displacement seen within multidrug-resistant S. sonnei lineages [16]. Sulfonamide resistance first appeared in S. flexneri isolates in the 1950s, followed by streptomycin and tetracycline resistance in the 1960s and β-lactam resistance in the 1970s [16]. The population history of S. sonnei contrasts significantly from that of S. flexneri. A pivotal study of 132 representative S. sonnei isolates demonstrated there are 3 major lineages that emerged within Europe <500 years ago [17]. S. sonnei is highly clonal, with roughly 10 000 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) found across these isolates. This is in marked contrast to S. flexneri, which has upward of 55 600 SNPs across 351 isolates [16]. The diversity of all S. sonnei isolates is roughly equivalent to the diversity seen within a single phylogenetic group in S. flexneri. Lineage III of S. sonnei, identified by Holt et al [17], has a much more recent common ancestor, dating to the 1970s, which is the primary clone that rapidly disseminated worldwide in the following decades. This study also suggests that acquisition of multidrug resistance loci within the global III lineage greatly facilitated this rapid global dispersal. Shigella species have been associated since the 1970s with sexual transmission among men who have sex with men (MSM). Over the past few decades, there has been increased isolation of S. flexneri (particularly serotype 3a) and S. sonnei within MSM communities in several countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia [18]. In 2009, S. flexneri serotype 3a was associated with an outbreak among MSM in the United Kingdom, which prompted Baker et al [19] to sequence a globally representative collection of 331 S. flexneri 3a isolates collected between 1995 and 2014. This studied illuminated that 1 main S. flexneri 3a lineage was circulating within the MSM community in the United Kingdom and had disseminated into other countries, such as Canada, Australia, and France. This MSM-associated lineage was also associated with resistance to azithromycin, which is used for primary treatment of multiple sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia, syphilis, and gonorrhea, but not for shigellosis [19]. This indicates that secondary selective pressure from coinfections resulted in the acquisition and maintenance of azithromycin resistance within the MSM-associated S. flexneri 3a lineage. Similarly, several studies have also used genomics to understand the sexual transmission of S. flexneri 2a and S. sonnei [20–22]. title: Defending ecology and evolution in an age of democratic backsliding and environmental crisis
authors: Dennis L. Murray
abstract: Frontiers journals encourage editors to publish perspectives pieces that overview the field and chart the journal's future direction. In my role as Field Chief Editor for Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution, I deviate from traditional format by offering a dire warning and urgent challenge to researchers, students, educators, and policymakers across ecology, evolution, and environmental science. Recent events at the confluence of democratic backsliding, erosion of academic institutions, and declining environmental governance threaten to radically alter the state of the world as we know it and our ability to sustain vigorous research and influence future policy decisions. If left unchecked, these converging forces will not simply hinder progress but bolster the dismantling of scientific capacity required to confront ongoing environmental crises. We must brace for impact by forcefully protecting the foundation of acquired knowledge, maintaining productive and relevant research in areas of global importance, and disseminating findings and expertise broadly so they are recognized as vital contributions to society. Given current trends across many liberal democracies, these are not small tasks.The last eight decades witnessed a Golden Age of scientific discovery, with nations mainly in the Western world and led by the United States, supporting transformational research across virtually all scientific disciplines (Baker, 2014;Powell et al., 2017). Notwithstanding prominent global inequities, developed nations advanced countless discoveries propelled by computational and technological advances that were previously unimaginable and that now fuel innumerable benefits to human health and prosperity (Dong et al., 2016;Coccia, 2023;Wang et al. 2023). Ecology and evolution experienced remarkable breakthroughs during this period, combining theoretical, observational, experimental, and analytical approaches to deepen our understanding of organismal function, variation, and interactions with the environment (Krebs, 2006;Bonsall and Charlesworth, 2010). Notably, these advances went beyond mere academic inquiry and also informed environmental policy and conservation efforts, helping manage species and ecosystems in the face of global change (Carpenter et al., 2009, Kareiva andMarvier, 2012). Such contributions are vital in light of ongoing biodiversity loss and climate crises that will intensify in the coming decades (Bellard et al., 2012;Segan et al., 2016).Recent history shows that scientific discovery and innovation are most successful and impactful in liberal democracies, where evidence-based scholarship is valued and governments support academia by protecting the right to teach, investigate, and disseminate knowledge without interference or censorship (Cole, 2017;Whetsell et al., 2021). In these systems, governments allocate public funds for infrastructure, salaries, and research while honouring institutional autonomy over governance and curricula. In return, academic institutions train the next generation of skilled professionals, conduct research and scholarship in areas of pressing societal importance, and provide knowledge and expertise through various forms of professional or public service. Yet, despite that democratic nations were well-served by this arrangement for decades, its long-term stability is increasingly in doubt. Since the early 2000s, many democracies have faced structural, economic, and governance challenges that threaten their integrity and place them on a path of democratic regression (Waldner and Lust, 2018;Diamond, 2021). The rise of populist and neonationalist movements, often fuelled by economic anxiety, cultural grievance, and demographic change, has shifted political power toward more repressive and authoritarian styles of governance (Galston, 2018;Berman, 2021). As these movements gain traction, they erode a healthy democracy's key features, including support for academic institutions and evidence-based policy decisions (Mede and Schäfer, 2020;V-Dem Institute, 2025; Figure 1). Almost universally, such movements depict universities as out of step with public needs, training students with ill-suited skills, and conducting expensive, esoteric research (Motta 2018;Merkley, 2020). These narratives resonate with segments of society lacking post-secondary education, allowing attacks on academia to be framed as fiscal prudence and reining-in the elite class (Gideon and Hall, 2017;Mede and Schäfer, 2020;Gligorić et al. 2025).The anti-democratic playbook includes measures designed to limit academia's societal influence, including restrictions on institutional funding, constraints on self-governance and curricular autonomy, threats to tenure and employment security, and curbs on free expression (Cole, 2017;Fernandez et al., 2024; Figure 2). Repressive governments often target research that does not align with official priorities or ideology, including basic curiosity-driven inquiry and investigations aimed at strengthening environmental needs. For example, research addressing evolutionary biology, environmental protection measures, climate change impacts, and at-risk species conservation tends to be valued in functioning democracies but frequently delegitimized in more repressive regimes (e.g., Rydén et al., 2019;Menezes and Barbosa, 2021;Frizelle et al., 2025;Temple, 2025). Research defunding may be framed as austerity measures or fiscal reallocations, often directing funds toward politically aligned programs while leaving other disciplines underresourced. Even when research funding is maintained, it is often more restrictive or administered through cost-sharing partnerships with business or special interest groups, thereby reducing efficiency and weakening direct links between objective academic inquiry and societal advancement (Dziundziuk, 2024;Pandey et al., 2025). Concurrently, populist and authoritarian movements often promote science skepticism and diminish the role of expert knowledge in policy decisions (Schlaufer and Van den Dool, 2024). When combined with reduced transparency and restricted public access to information, these measures erode public trust in institutions and reduce engagement in policy processes (Hernández-Huerta and Inclán, 2025). Collectively, such strategies weaken the autonomy and influence of academic institutions and progressively decouple research activity from the broader societal needs it is intended to serve (Figure 2).An additional feature of democratic regression is that emerging regimes frequently prioritize economic growth over environmental protection and sustainability (Pentz et al., 2025; Figure 1). As the administrative state and public service are weakened or dismantled, environmental oversight and regulations are often removed, relaxed, or inconsistently enforced (Blum and Sellers, 2025), resulting in reduced environmental monitoring, declining quality standards, and diminished protection for sensitive habitats and at-risk species (Kates-Garnick, 2025; Meek and Börk, 2025;Shiffman, 2025;Orr, 2025). Activities such as basic research, monitoring, and assessment of species and ecosystems are particularly vulnerable, whether conducted directly by government agencies or through partnerships with academia and non-governmental organizations (Böhmelt, 2021;Halligan, 2021;Lockwood and Lockwood, 2022). Consequently, data on environmental baselines, human impacts, and mitigation strategies becomes less accessible (e.g., Dillon et al., 2019) while expert involvement in policy decisions is increasingly devalued, leading to weakened evidence-based environmental governance. Collectively, these losses activate a feedback loop promoting increased public detachment from environmental governance and policy, thereby reinforcing populist sentiments in society (Figure 2). It follows that losses in environmental research and policy in one nation can extend to other countries given the large spatial scale of many environmental problems and frequent need for coordinated scientific and regulatory responses (Steffen et al., 2015). Thus, ongoing and predicted increases in global biodiversity loss and climate change impacts place society in a perfect storm with far fewer scientific and regulatory guardrails.Democratic losses and related impacts on academia and the environment are well-documented in countries such as Hungary, Turkey, India, and Russia (Sundar, 2018;Ignatieff, 2023;Grigoriadis and Canpolat, 2024), but similar trends, often less overt, are present in nearly all major democracies worldwide. Over the past two decades, the majority of G20 nations, representing roughly 85% of global GDP, 75% of international trade, and 67% of the world's population, have exhibited signs of democratic regression (Diamond, 2020;Williamson et al., 2025), declining support for academic institutions (Fernandez et al., 2024;Lott, 2024;Hernández-Huerta & Inclán, 2025), and weakening environmental oversight (Pentz et al., 2025; see Supplementary Figure 1). Countries that recently signed international agreements to curb greenhouse gas emissions or expand land and water protection have quietly backtracked on their commitments (Lamb et al., 2020;Roelfsema et al., 2020;Roberts, 2024;Specht, 2025). In most cases, national priorities now emphasize economic growth and defence spending over support for higher education or environmental protection.These changes extend far beyond a simple rightward political shift. Even nations traditionally viewed as exemplars of liberal democracy, including my own country, Canada, classified as a "Full Democracy" (see Economist Intelligence Unit, 2014; 2024) and celebrated for freedom and environmental stewardship, have gradually slipped in measures of democratic performance and academic and environmental protection (see Savoie, 2019;Erl, 2020;Stockemeyer and Gaspard, 2025; Evidence for Democracy, 2025; Supplementary Figure 1). Indeed, Canada is increasingly reliant on private-public partnerships to support academic research (Canadian Association of University Teachers n.d.), which especially harms 'basic' research productivity because of its lessened link to revenue generation or societal benefit. Canada is increasingly supported by environmental policy outcomes with political rather than evidence-based motivations (Piper et al., 2022;Migone et al., 2024), imposes various forms of interference on government scientists working on environmental issues (Turner, 2013;Robertson et al., 2023), and has surprisingly weak environmental standards and governance (Cooke et al., 2016;OECD, 2017;Gibson et al., 2019;Ray et al., 2021). Canada's quiet backtracking on international commitments, such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and its retreat from Paris Climate Accord targets, represent an insidious version of the overt assaults on environmental governance seen in less democratic nations.More dramatically and impactfully, the United States is in the midst of a slide into full-blown authoritarianism, with attendant erosion of its basic democratic, academic and environmental standards (Carrier and Carothers, 2025;Scholars at Risk, 2025) and uncertainty as to whether this trend will soon be reversed (Fernandez and Hutchens, 2025). Meanwhile, China's ascent as a global superpower offers little reassurance given its undeniable authoritarian structure and low rankings in key democratic and environmental metrics (Economist Intelligence Unit 2014; V-Dem Institute, 2025). Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 1 synthesize these trends, illustrating how democratic backsliding is broadly associated with declines in academic freedom and environmental performance across regime types. Although some democratic nations retain the potential to provide global leadership on matters of democracy and the environment that are currently neglected by superpower nations, most face domestic challenges that limit their capacity to act forcefully. Thus, the global nature of current biodiversity and climate crises, transcending national borders and political regimes, will require unconventional responses if we are to avert a profoundly dark period in human history.A variety of strategies exist for resisting democratic regression and reversing authoritarian encroachment, and academics like Hannah Arendt, Bertrand Russell, and Timothy Snyder exemplify the long tradition of intellectual resistance to anti-democratic forces (Said, 1994). While such engagement has historically been more common in the humanities and social sciences, natural scientists tend to be less engaged and may encounter greater structural or reputational barriers to public advocacy (e.g., Rodrigues et al., 2023). Nevertheless, for researchers, educators, and policy specialists in ecology, evolution, and related fields, engagement should be viewed as necessary and may involve forming broad, sometimes unorthodox coalitions to strengthen democratic foundations and safeguard academic integrity and research, while simultaneously reinforcing public trust in institutions and evidence-based decision-making. The strategies outlined below are broadly applicable across disciplines and draw inspiration from humanities and social science research on best practices for countering democratic backslide and resisting authoritarianism (Acemoglu and Robinson, 2012;Snyder, 2017Snyder, , 2018;;Gamboa, 2022;Johnson et al., 2024;Bunce et al., 2025).Data purges and disinformation. Public data accessibility and integrity are at risk in declining democracies, with information from sources such as government environmental monitoring programs or partnerships with other entities being especially vulnerable. Authoritarian regimes tend not to adhere to FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable) standards (O'Connor et al., 2019), and environmental datasets can be selectively removed or altered (Grigoriadis and Canpolat, 2024). Hungary ended longitudinal analysis of key air and water quality datasets while Turkey's repressions removed key personnel responsible for monitoring endangered species (Böhmelt, 2021;Halligan, 2021). These disruptions delayed critical biodiversity assessments and reduced data availability for global climate models, illustrating the broad consequences of data suppression and targeted academic repression on research continuity.In response to such actions, coalitions can work to protect public data, ensuring that datasets and findings remain broadly available in the future. title: Primary care management of allergic rhinitis in children
authors: Amanda Loke; Lee Gan Goh; Rajeev Ramachandran
abstract: Opening Vignette Lionel, an 11-year-old boy, was brought by his mother to your clinic for longstanding nasal blockage and snoring. Lionel’s mother reported that he had been having constant nasal blockage for the past 2 years, as well as bouts of sneezing attacks. She also noticed that he ground his teeth at night, resulting in recurrent mouth ulcers. The patient reported poor night-time sleep with resultant daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating in school. He did not have symptoms suggestive of sleep apnoea, such as loud snoring with pauses in breathing or choking in sleep, or frequent upper respiratory tract infections. He had a history of mild eczema as an infant but did not require pharmacotherapy. There was a significant family history of atopy, with both parents having had asthma. During physical examination, you noticed a transverse crease on the dorsum of the patient’s nose resulting from constant rubbing. He also had pale oedematous inferior turbinates with clear watery discharge. Examination of the oral cavity did not reveal any enlarged tonsils, and the ear examination was normal.WHAT IS ALLERGIC RHINITIS? Allergic rhinitis (AR) is a chronic symptomatic disorder of the nose that arises after exposure to allergens via immunoglobulin-E (IgE)-mediated Type 1 hypersensitivity reactions. This results in inflammation of the lining of the nose.[1] Common allergens include house dust mite, dander from animals such as cats and dogs, mould and cockroach waste. Based on the Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma (ARIA) guidelines, AR can be classified by the temporal pattern (e.g. intermittent or persistent) and by severity (mild or moderate–severe).[2] Severity of AR is classified as mild when symptoms are present but do not interfere with quality of life. It is classified as severe when symptoms are significant enough to interfere with quality of life, for example, sleep disturbance, impairment of daily activities and impairment of school performance. Figure 1 classifies AR according to the ARIA guidelines.Figure 1: Classification of allergic rhinitis according to the Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma guidelines. Allergic rhinitis can be categorised based on symptom duration (intermittent, persistent) and severity (mild, moderate/severe).HOW RELEVANT IS THIS TO MY PRACTICE? Allergic rhinitis is the most common chronic disease in childhood, affecting up to 25% of children,[3] with a peak prevalence in the adolescent years.[4] In Singapore, due to the tropical climate year-round, which promotes the proliferation of dust mites and mould, most people with AR have the persistent type.[5] In addition, house dust mite is the most common allergen trigger, as the majority of the local population is sensitised to it.[6] Symptoms that children with AR typically present with include nasal congestion, sneezing, rhinorrhoea and itching. However, they may also present with atypical symptoms via associated comorbidities, depending on the child’s age. Some of these atypical presentations include recurrent ear infections and reduced hearing due to eustachian tube dysfunction, cough, poorly controlled asthma, sleep problems, poor concentration at school, prolonged and frequent respiratory tract infections, and impairment of school performance.[7] In the paediatric population, the physician may also observe a phenomenon known as ‘atopic march’, which refers to the sequential development of atopic conditions over the course of infancy and childhood. The typical atopic march sequence begins with atopic dermatitis in infancy, progressing to food allergy, asthma and AR. In light of this and considering that a period of allergen exposure is required before the development of the disease, it is rare for children under 2 years of age to have AR. As such, if a very young child appears to have persistent nasal symptoms, other diagnoses should be considered. Likewise, unilateral symptoms, mucopurulent rhinorrhoea, anosmia and pain are also unlikely to be due to AR, and other diagnoses should be considered. WHAT CAN I DO IN MY PRACTICE? Clinicians should devote time to the diagnosis and management of children presenting with signs and symptoms of AR. Quick-relief medications such as decongestants, for example, oxymetazoline, provide short-term symptom relief but not lasting long-term control, and hence should be avoided. Overall, AR requires more of the physician’s time to diagnose and manage successfully. Recognising allergic rhinitis in children Diagnosing AR in the paediatric population presents unique challenges. This is because children are often unable to verbalise their symptoms, resulting in the condition remaining undiagnosed and untreated. As such, it is important for a physician to recognise the signs that point to AR. These include ‘allergic shiners’ (dark circles around the eyes related to venodilation), ‘allergic salute’ (the continual habit of rubbing the nose in an upward or transverse manner) and ‘allergic crease’ (a horizontal crease across the lower half of the bridge of the nose resulting from the continual upward rubbing of the nose). The clinical history should include the symptom type, chronicity of symptoms, frequency of symptoms, exacerbating factors, severity of symptoms and family history of atopy. Nasal congestion is a prominent symptom in children and may be the only complaint. The caregiver may also bring to attention symptoms such as watery rhinorrhoea, frequent sneezing, a nasal voice, repeated throat clearing, mouth breathing, frequent snoring or chronic gaping of the mouth. Other presenting symptoms due to uncontrolled AR could be recurrent headache from sinusitis, early morning abdominal discomfort from aerophagia and mouth breathing, cough, recurrent oral ulcers and teeth enamel erosions from teeth grinding, malalignment of teeth, and inattention at school. Allergic rhinitis is usually not considered a possible cause of these symptoms; as a result, the patient often undergoes unnecessary testing and treatment without any improvement in symptoms. Physical examination findings The nose, tympanic membrane and oropharynx should be examined, as they may show findings suggestive of AR or other associated conditions. A standard office otoscopy should be used to visualise the nasal mucosa and the appearance of the turbinates. Nasal obstruction is often seen, and the turbinates may be enlarged or swollen with pale nasal mucosa and clear nasal secretions. The oral cavity should also be examined, looking out for pharyngeal cobblestoning and enlarged tonsils. However, it is pertinent to note that negative examination findings do not eliminate the possibility of AR. COMMON PITFALLS IN MANAGEMENT The control of AR is often suboptimal due to poor adherence to medications on the patient’s or caregiver’s part, poor understanding of disease and inadequate follow-up.[8] Sufficient emphasis should be placed on patient and/or caregiver education to empower them for chronic management. Common parental misconceptions It is important to correct misconceptions about AR through parental education; this will help to prevent trivialising of symptoms or nonadherence to treatment. Common myths include views that AR is harmless and that all children will outgrow their allergies. It must be noted that although the nature of the symptoms of AR is non-life-threatening, they can have a major effect on quality of life, sleep, academic performance, emotional well-being and productivity when poorly controlled. In addition, untreated AR can contribute to potentially serious sequelae, including asthma, sinusitis and recurrent otitis media. Majority of children diagnosed with AR will have symptoms 10 years later, and 40% of young adults will have them even 20 years later.[9] Another misconception is that physicians may prescribe inappropriate or ineffective doses of medications and may not provide adequate follow-up to assess response to treatment. Parents may also have the belief that testing for allergen-specific IgE with blood tests or skin testing before making the presumptive diagnosis of AR and initiating treatment is unnecessary. Indeed, the identification of possible triggers through a good clinical history and initiation of empirical treatment are sufficient for most patients. However, the caveat is that there should be adequate follow-up to assess the patient’s response to treatment. Patients who have refractory symptoms should be referred to a paediatric allergist for further evaluation, or an alternative diagnosis should be considered. MANAGING ALLERGIC RHINITIS IN CHILDREN The management strategies of AR in children include avoidance of allergens, pharmacotherapy and use of specific immunotherapy (IT). Partnership between patients, caregivers and the medical team is also essential for the effective treatment of AR. The World Health Organization developed the ARIA guidelines to provide clinicians with an evidence-based resource for the management of both adults and children with AR. The guidelines, which suggest a stepwise approach to treatment to maximise the benefits of treatment while minimising adverse side effects, have been adapted and illustrated in Figure 2.Figure 2: Care pathway for the management of allergic rhinitis. Adapted from the Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma 2008 guidelines.Allergen avoidance Avoidance of allergen triggers is recommended where possible. However, a more realistic goal would be to decrease allergen exposure as much as possible. The physician should also be mindful that major environmental modifications, such as removing carpeting and replacing upholstered furniture, are expensive and might not be affordable for all families. To enhance patient and caregiver cooperation, initial emphasis should be placed on low-cost interventions. Practical strategies to reduce exposure to common allergens in Singapore are outlined in Box 1.Box 1: Practical strategies to reduce exposure to common allergens in Singapore.Pharmacological treatment Medications for AR are generally necessary, as complete allergen avoidance is not always feasible. Pharmacotherapy aims at safe and effective symptom relief with prevention of complications. Oral antihistamines Oral antihistamines help to reduce symptoms of rhinorrhoea and nasal itch but do not help with nasal congestion.[10] Second-generation antihistamines are preferred because they are comparable in efficacy with an improved side effect profile and longer duration of action. First-generation antihistamines can be useful at night to help with sleep. However, they are generally not recommended due to their ability to cross the blood–brain barrier, which results in side effects such as sedation and difficulty with learning.[10] Oral and nasal decongestants Both oral and nasal decongestants are available in Singapore. They alleviate nasal congestion but do not help with nasal itch and rhinorrhoea.[11] They are also ineffective in providing durable long-term control of AR. When used in combination with oral antihistamines for short-duration therapy, they offer some short-term symptom control. If used longer than 3–5 days, topical decongestants run the risk of causing rebound congestion and ‘stuffiness’. They should not be used for control of chronic symptoms. Table 1 shows the common antihistamines and decongestants available in Singapore that are safe for use in the paediatric population.Table 1: Antihistamines and decongestants that are safe for use in the paediatric population.aIntranasal antihistamines Intranasal antihistamines such as azelastine and olopatadine have been shown to be effective in rapidly improving nasal congestion in children.[11] However, intranasal sprays are generally not actively marketed in Singapore. Azelastine is registered for use in Singapore as a combination nasal spray with fluticasone propionate for children 12 years and older, while olopatadine as an intranasal spray is currently not available. Intranasal corticosteroids Intranasal corticosteroids are effective in relieving nasal congestion, rhinorrhoea and nasal itch, and are recommended for patients with moderate to severe symptoms.[12] They do not work instantly, as the maximal effect may require several days or weeks of regular use to be apparent. Treatment should be started at the maximal dose appropriate for age, and the dose can be tapered down gradually to the lowest effective dose. Subsequently, patients can reduce the frequency of dose gradually and maintain symptom control with use as needed. Studies show that intranasal corticosteroids are relatively safe in children and do not influence long-term growth velocity due to the relatively low doses used in nasal sprays.[12] However, physicians should still monitor the growth of any child on long-term corticosteroid-containing medications. Other potential side effects include epistaxis and nasal septum perforation, and hence, the proper technique of administration needs to be taught to patients and/or their caregivers. Intranasal corticosteroids of any type should be tapered to the lowest effective dose in all patients once symptoms are controlled. Commonly used intranasal steroids in Singapore that are safe for use in the paediatric population are listed in Table 2.Table 2: Common intranasal steroids in Singapore that are safe for use in the paediatric population.aBest recommendations for administration are as follows: begin by blowing the nose gently, lean the head forward and ensure that the nasal spray is almost vertical. Patients are advised to use the hand opposite the nostril being treated, aim the nozzle upwards and outwards pointing towards the ear of the nostril being treated, and spray without sniffing. Following administration, patients should be advised to rinse the mouth and throat. For younger children who need help, caregivers could get the child to sit down while they stand or squat in front of them. The child should be instructed to look down like they are reading a book, while the caregiver aims the nozzle upwards and outwards.[13] A common cause of treatment failure is poor technique when administering intranasal corticosteroids. Hence, it is important for physicians to spend time explaining the appropriate use of these devices. Intranasal decongestants Intranasal decongestants, such as oxymetazoline, are commonly prescribed for relief of nasal congestion. However, they only offer some improved symptom control in the short term. In addition, they carry the risk of systemic side effects, including hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, palpitations and central nervous system excitation.[12] Also, if used for longer than 3–5 days, intranasal decongestants may cause rebound congestion and stuffiness. They should not be used for control of chronic symptoms. Leukotriene receptor antagonists Montelukast should not be used as a primary treatment therapy for AR due to concerns about the risk–benefit profile. Neuropsychiatric effects, such as serious behaviour and mood-related changes, have been reported in association with the use of montelukast. However, they are uncommon. Nevertheless, its use should be restricted as an add-on therapy for patients with inadequate response or intolerance to alternative therapies.[12] Other measures: saline douching Nasal saline irrigation, also known as nasal douche, is a procedure that rinses the nasal cavity with saline solutions. Some patients may find it helpful to reduce symptoms and improve the effect of nasal steroids. It has been shown to be effective and tolerable in the majority of children and can be considered along with pharmacotherapy.[14] If saline douching is done, it should be done before intranasal corticosteroid use to avoid rinsing out the intranasal corticosteroid and rendering it ineffective. Cost considerations Due to the chronic nature of AR requiring medium- to long-term usage of medications, it is important to keep health affordable for patients. In Singapore, mometasone furoate (Nasonex™) and triamcinolone acetonide (Nasacort®) have recently been added to the subsidised drug list. This lowers retail price from over SGD 20 to about SGD 10 per bottle (140 metered actuations). Fluticasone furoate (Avamys™) remains unsubsidised. When selecting medications, physicians should keep in mind that choosing a cheaper drug may improve access and long-term adherence for patients with financial constraints. Specific immunotherapy Specific allergy IT is a treatment option for children with AR. Subcutaneous IT and sublingual IT can be considered for children aged >5 years. Indications include uncontrolled significant rhinitis symptoms despite appropriate pharmacological management, intolerance to medications or a desire to decrease long-term medication use. When administered appropriately, IT has been shown to successfully decrease symptoms of AR during the treatment period. However, patients need to be committed to a minimum treatment period of 3 years. This duration is generally recommended to ensure lasting benefits after cessation of IT and to reduce relapse rates.[15] WHEN SHOULD I REFER TO A SPECIALIST? Referral to an allergist should be considered in children with moderate to severe AR and prolonged or severe symptoms of rhinitis despite adequate pharmacotherapy and allergen avoidance. Patients with significant complications of AR, such as recurrent sinusitis or recurrent otitis media, should also be referred to an allergist. Referral should also be considered for patients who are interested to discuss IT as a treatment option. TAKE HOME MESSAGES Allergic rhinitis is a chronic atopic condition commonly encountered in the primary care setting. Physicians should be aware and recognise the various ways that AR can present in children. Management strategies of AR include allergen avoidance, pharmacotherapy and specific allergy IT. A stepwise approach should be taken in the pharmacological management of patients. Adequate follow-up is essential to assess treatment response and to ensure that the dose of intranasal steroids is tapered to the lowest effective dose once symptoms are controlled. Effective partnership between patients, caregivers and physicians is crucial for the successful treatment of AR. Referral to a specialist should be considered in children with severe symptoms of AR despite adequate pharmacotherapy and allergen avoidance, those with significant complications of AR and those who are keen to consider IT as a treatment option. Closing Vignette Lionel was diagnosed with moderate–persistent AR based on the clinical history and physical examination. Lionel and his mother were educated about AR, and the patient was started on a 4-week trial of intranasal corticosteroids. After 4 weeks of adequate treatment, his symptoms improved. The dose of intranasal corticosteroids was tapered down and continued for two more months. A further follow-up was arranged subsequently.Acknowledgement We greatly appreciate the support of the Department of Family Medicine, National University Health Systems, Singapore. https://doi.org/10.31635/ccschem.019.20190010 SectionsAboutAbstractPDF ToolsAdd to favoritesDownload CitationsTrack Citations ShareFacebookTwitterLinked InEmail Tumor hypoxia is one of the hostile tumor microenvironment characteristics occurring in solid tumors. This feature is closely related to tumor progression and can negatively impair the effectiveness of cancer therapeutics. Recently, various strategies have been developed that enable efficient tumor oxygenation, not only enhancing treatment outcome of oxygen-consuming cancer therapeutics such as radiotherapy and photodynamic therapy, but also reversing the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment to promote cancer immunotherapy. This review focuses on the latest progress in design and fabrication of innovative tumor-targeted oxygen nanoshuttles that attenuate tumor hypoxia and enhance cancer therapy. Future perspectives for clinical translation of tumor-targeted oxygen nanoshuttles will be further discussed. Download figure Download PowerPoint Introduction Tumor hypoxia, together with low pH values, excess extracellular matrix, and immunosuppressive factors, among others, are common hostile features of the solid tumor microenvironment (TME) resulting from altered metabolic pathways and abnormal tumor vasculature.1–3 Accumulating evidence indicates that the hypoxic TME plays a pivotal role in promoting tumor growth. It also significantly attenuates response of tumor cells to various cancer treatments, including radiotherapy and chemotherapy.4–8 Moreover, severe tumor hypoxia endows solid tumors with immunosuppressive TME features that disable the host immune system from detecting of the tumor and thus reducing the effects of immunotherapy.9–11 There is thus an increased need for effective strategies that address tumor hypoxia. With the rapid advancement of nanotechnology, a variety of nanoformulations with unique physiochemical properties have recently been designed for enhanced cancer treatment by promoting tumor oxygenation or depleting tumor oxygen, since oxygen plays a pivotal role in the cancer development and treatment.12–16 Recent studies have shown that catalytic nanoformulations that reach tumor cells decompose the high-endogenous H2O2 levels and generate O2, thus effectively attenuating tumor hypoxia.17–19 Such nanoformulations enhance treatment outcomes of oxygen-consuming cancer radiotherapy and photodynamic therapy (PDT), as well as promote a therapeutic response to immune checkpoint blockade therapy by modulating the immunosuppressive TME.20–26 Other pioneering strategies have used various nanoformulations to deliver compounds that inhibit oxygen consumption in tumor cells, thus increasing tumor oxygenation and leading to improved results with PDT.27,28 Another promising strategy for efficient tumor oxygenation is the increase of oxygen supply within tumors.29,30 Inspired by artificial blood cell substitutes, several groups have recently designed different types of tumor-targeted oxygen-delivery nanoshuttles.31,32 In this review, we will describe the design of these different nanoshuttles, mechanisms underlying their mode of action, their effect on tumor oxygenation, and their efficacy for improving various cancer treatments (summarized in Table 1). Table 1 | A Summary of Oxygen Nanoshuttles for Tumor Oxygenation and Cancer Therapy Enhancement Shuttle Type Fabrication Method Applications References Hemoglobin-based oxygen nanoshuttles Noncovalent encapsulation PDT [33] Chemotherapy [34] Covalent hybridization/conjugation PDT [35,33] Immunotherapy [36] PFC-based oxygen nanoshuttles Nanodroplets stabilized with lipids or HSA molecules Radiotherapy [37–39] PDT [37,40,41] Encapsulation within a red blood cell membrane "ghost" Radiotherapy [42] PDT [41] Loading with hollow nanoparticles Radiotherapy [43–45] Sonodynamic therapy [46] Fluorinated COPs PDT [47] MOF-based oxygen nanoshuttles UiO-66 MOFs PDT [48] Oxygen precursors CaO2/catalase-encapsulated alginate pellets Chemotherapy [49] H2O2-encapsulated liposomes Radioimmunotherapy [20] Approaches to Oxygen Nanoshuttles Design Hemoglobin, a protein consisting of four subunits each with a heme group and a globin chain, is the oxygen carrier within red blood cells.50 Hemoglobin-based artificial blood substitutes have been extensively explored over the past few decades,31 inspiring development of hemoglobin-based nanoformulations for tumor-targeted oxygen delivery.51 Such nanoformulations show passive tumor homing via the enhanced permeability and retention effect, leading to efficient tumor oxygenation.35,52,53 Cai and co-workers34,36,54 have encapsulated hemoglobin within either poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles, lipids, or cancer cell membranes and have also formed intermolecular disulfide bonds of hemoglobin and reduced human serum albumin (HSA) to create hybrid hemoglobin-based oxygen nanocarriers. In addition, Zhang and co-workers55 have coated polydopamine-encapsulated hemoglobin with a red blood cell membrane "ghost," thus achieving man-made red blood cells for tumor-targeted oxygen shuttling that enhances cancer treatment. Another type of widely explored artificial blood substitute is represented by nanoemulsions based on perfluorocarbon (PFC), owing to this compound's high oxygen-dissolving capacity, low immunogenicity, and excellent physiochemical stability.32 Several research groups, including ours, have designed such PFC nanoemulsions, stabilized with lipids or HSA molecules.37,40 Moreover, to exploit the long circulation time of red blood cells, we and others have designed PFC nanoemulsions encapsulated within red blood cell membrane "ghosts" as stable biomimetic oxygen nanoshuttles.56,57 In addition, various mesoporous nanostructures such as hollow Bi2Se3 or mesoporous organosilica nanostructures perfused with PFC have been demonstrated to be effective in promoting tumor oxygenation for enhanced radiotherapy or sonodynamic therapy.43,44,46 Our group has also developed a type of fluorinated covalent organic polymer (COP) cross-linked with perfluorosebacic acid, thereby enabling efficient PFC loading and tumor oxygenation.47 Hu and co-workers38,58,59 have recently reported that albumin or liposomal nanoformulations loaded with a unique type of PFC, perfluorotributylamine, can inhibit tumor-associated platelets, leading to disruption of tumor vessel barriers and thereby increased red blood cell infiltration, which enables synergistic tumor oxygenation. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are an emerging class of crystalline materials comprised of inorganic metal ion nodes bound via organic linkers. Owing to their characteristic mesoporous structure, MOFs have been extensively explored for gas storage, separation, and sensing, as well as controllable drug delivery in biomedical applications.60,61 Several types of MOFs have recently shown promise as sorbent materials for oxygen storage.62,63 More recently, Gao et al.48 used a MOF nanoplatform based on zirconium(IV), oxygen-storing material, to deliver oxygen to the tumor site via the enhanced permeability and retention effect. Peroxides such as H2O2 can be converted to molecular oxygen in the presence of catalase.64 Thus, nanoshuttles loaded with catalase have been used to catalytically decompose excess endogenous H2O2 within solid tumors and promote tumor oxygenation.17,18 Moreover, recent studies have delivered nanoparticles loaded with catalase either separately or together with oxygen precursors (e.g., H2O2, CaO2), to serve as oxygen-generating depots at tumors.20,49 The next sections will classify currently developed nanoshuttles according to their use for enhancing various cancer treatments: PDT, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy. Oxygen Nanoshuttles for Enhanced PDT Photodynamic therapy is a promising noninvasive technique for the treatment of many tumor types. This technique uses excitation light and photosensitizers to generate reactive singlet oxygen from molecular oxygen and thus induce cell death.65 However, owing to the severe tumor hypoxia of most solid tumors, current PDT treatment outcomes are still far from satisfactory.2 Early strategies for improving PDT efficacy commonly focused on enhancing tumor accumulation of photosensitizers or synthesizing new photosensitizers with increased singlet oxygen quantum yield and longer excitation wavelength.66 Later efforts have focused on improving intratumoral oxygen concentration, another key component for PDT.29 In 2015, Hu and co-workers40 prepared oxygen self-enriching nanophotosensitizers by coencapsulating the near-infrared (NIR) photosensitizer IR780 and perfluorohexane (PFH) within lipid nanodroplets. PFH has high oxygen-dissolving capacity and thus enriches molecular oxygen for photodynamic consumption by IR780; it also protects the PDT-produced singlet oxygen from decay, thus synergistically improving singlet oxygen quantum yield of IR780 and extending its action time. Following intravenous injection, the PFH nanodroplets were shown to overcome hypoxia-induced resistance to PDT and inhibit tumor growth in mice. We have recently developed fluorinated COPs synthesized via one-pot esterification by cross-linking perfluorosebacic acid and polyethylene glycol with the photosensitizer meso-5,10,15,20-tetra (4-hydroxylphenyl) porphyrin (THPP) (Figure 1).47 Due to the mesoporous structure of perfluorosebacic acid, these THPPpf-PEG nano-COPs showed efficient loading of a PFC variant, perfluoro-15-crown-5-ether (PFCE), enabling molecular oxygen together with THPP. Intravenously injected PFCE-loaded THPPpf-PEG enhanced PDT in tumor-bearing mice, probably due to nanoparticle absorbance of oxygen when passing through the lungs, and its gradual release upon tumor accumulation, which attenuated tumor hypoxia. Figure 1 | Long circulating fluorinated nano-COPs for tumor-targeted oxygen delivery and enhanced PDT. (a) Schematic illustration of the synthesis process of fluorinated COPs and subsequent PFCE loading. (b) Scheme illustrating the tumor oxygenation process, during which PFCE-loaded THPPpf-PEG would efficiently absorb oxygen when passing through the lungs and then gradually release the loaded oxygen when accumulated inside tumors to endow efficient tumor hypoxia attenuation. (c) Photoacoustic imaging of tumors upon mice that received systemic administration of plain THPPpf-PEG and PFCE-loaded THPPpf-PEG at indicated time points post injection. (d) Ex vivo immunofluorescence staining of tumor slices of tumor-bearing mice that received systemic administration of plain THPPpf-PEG and PFCE-loaded THPPpf-PEG at varying time points using external pimonidazole as the hypoxia probe. (e) In vivo tumor growth curves of mice after various treatments, as indicated. Originally published by Tao and co-workers47 and approved for reuse by John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Download figure Download PowerPoint Other types of oxygen nanoshuttles formulated with hemoglobin, or zirconium(IV)-based MOFs, have also been shown to enhance the photodynamic effects of coloaded photosynthesizers (e.g., chlorin e6 [Ce6] or indocyanine green).48,33 Gao et al.48 reported that the zirconium(IV)-based MOFs, which exhibited high loading capacity toward both oxygen and indocyanine green (ICG) molecules, showed burst release of oxygen inside tumors upon NIR light exposure, thereby significantly improving the photodynamic efficacy of ICG in the hypoxic regions. Therefore, elevating oxygen concentrations inside tumors is a promising strategy for enhancing PDT treatment outcomes. Oxygen Nanoshuttles for Enhanced Radiotherapy Radiotherapy, either by external radiation (e.g., via X-rays, γ-rays, electrons) or by internal radiation with implantable radioactive isotopes (brachytherapy), is a well-known cancer treatment modality generally used alongside surgery and chemotherapy.67 Molecular oxygen, an extremely electron-affinic molecule, fixates the DNA damage induced by radiation, which leads to tumor cell apoptosis.68 Thus, tumor oxygen concentrations have a crucial role in the therapeutic outcome of radiotherapies.69 Over the past decades, clinical trials have made different attempts to address resistance to radiotherapy caused by tumor hypoxia, for example, via hyperbaric oxygen breathing.70 More recently, we prepared HSA-stabilized PFC nanodroplets for attenuating tumor hypoxia and thus enhanced radiotherapy (Figure 2a).37 Following intravenous injection of the PFC nanodroplets, tumors in mice under hyperbaric oxygen breathing presented significantly improved oxygenation, as visualized with photoacoustic imaging. Simultaneously, tumor-localized ultrasound stimulation was performed to boost release of the loaded oxygen and of oxygen adsorbed by the nanodroplets when circulating through the lungs. This approach led to efficient tumor hypoxia attenuation, enhancing therapeutic efficacy of both X-ray-based radiotherapy and Ce6-mediated PDT, in different tumor xenograft models. Figure 2 | PFC-based oxygen nanoshuttles for stimuli-responsive tumor oxygenation and enhanced PDT and radiotherapy. (a) Schematic illustration showing tumor-bearing mice that received intravenous injection of HSA-stabilized PFC nanodroplets followed by hyperbaric oxygen breathing and tumor-localized ultrasound stimulation. Treatments attenuated tumor hypoxia and enhanced response to both PDT and radiotherapy. The figure was originally published by Song et al.37 and was approved for reuse by ACS Publishing group. (b) Preparation of PFC-loaded hollow Bi2Se3 nanoparticles for NIR light-responsive tumor oxygenation and enhanced cancer radiotherapy. The figure was originally published by Song et al.44 and was approved for reuse by John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Download figure Download PowerPoint Another factor that severely impairs radiotherapy treatment outcome is limited absorption cross-section of radiation beams.62 Therefore, an alternative radiosensitization strategy is to deposit high Z-element-containing materials (e.g., Au) within solid tumors.17,69 Our group has prepared hollow Bi2Se3 nanostructures, via a facile one-pot cation exchange method and Kirkendall effect using small MnSe nanoparticles as a template, and loaded with PFH under reduced pressure, to serve as oxygen nanoshuttles.44 Following intratumoral injection of the particles to tumor-bearing mice and treatment with a 808 nm laser, the strong NIR absorbance of Bi2Se3 elevated the local temperature over the evaporation point of PFH, thereby modulating the oxygen release rate and promoting tumor oxygenation (Figure 2b). This remotely controllable NIR-induced tumor oxygenation, together with the capacity of Bi as a high Z element for radiosensitization, yielded a synergistically enhanced antitumor effect. Long, circulating PFC-based nanoshuttles, such as red blood cell membrane "ghosts" enveloping [email protected] nanoparticles,42 were shown to attenuate tumor hypoxia in mice due to efficient tumor accumulation, and without requiring external stimulation, ultimately enhancing cancer radiotherapy. These studies reveal that tumor oxygenation is a promising strategy for radiotherapy sensitization. Oxygen Nanoshuttles for Enhanced Chemotherapy The treatment outcome of chemotherapy, another widely used treatment in the clinic, also correlates with intratumoral oxygen concentrations.71 Tumor hypoxia has a detrimental effect on delivery of chemodrugs to distant hypoxic zones and on their subsequent cellular uptake, and also impairs the generation of reactive oxygen species from molecular oxygen by several chemo drugs (e.g., doxorubicin [DOX], oxaliplatin), which hinders their ability to induce cell death.72 Moreover, tumor hypoxia induces proteomic and genomic adaptations causing tumor cells to develop into more malignant phenotypes, which can lead to more severe chemoresistance.72,73 A recent pioneering study showed that improved tumor oxygenation with hyperbaric oxygen breathing increases sensitization of hypoxic cells to DOX and other chemodrugs.74 In a recent work by Sung and co-workers49, the authors prepared an implantable oxygen-generating depot by adding an alginate solution containing the oxygen precursor, CaO2, and catalase to a CaCl2 bath, which yielded Ca2+-cross-linked microencapsulated pellets. Upon implantation close to the tumor region, the CaO2 reacts with water that infiltrates the pellet from interstitial tissues, forming calcium hydroxide and H2O2; the latter, via coencapsulated catalase, decomposes to produce molecular oxygen. As a result, these tumor-localized, oxygen-generating depots increase response to intravenously administered DOX. For more effective and tumor-targeted oxygen delivery, Cai and co-workers75 recently constructed tumor-homologous targeting oxygen nanoshuttles, by loading PLGA-encapsulated hemoglobin and DOX within tumor cell membranes (Figure 3). Due to the tumor cell adhesion molecules upon their surface, these nanoshuttles increased tumor homing efficiency following intravenous injection, leading to effective tumor hypoxia attenuation. This, in turn, led to downregulation of hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, multidrug resistance gene 1, and P-glycoprotein, important factors involved in exocytosis of DOX; thus, these nanoshuttles increased the antitumor efficacy of chemotherapy in mice. Figure 3 | Hemoglobin-based oxygen nanoshuttles for tumor oxygenation and enhanced chemotherapy. (a) Scheme showing preparation of DOX/Hb loaded PLGA-cancer cell membrane nanoparticles (DHCNPs). (b) Scheme showing utilization of the DHCNPs for effective tumor oxygenation via homologous targeting and subsequent downregulation of HIF-1α, MDR1, and P-gp for enhanced chemotherapeutic efficacy of DOX. (c) Ex vivo immunofluorescence hypoxia staining of tumor slices collected from mice at 24 h post intravenous injection of DHCNPs. (d) P-gp expression levels of tumors with or without oxygenation treatment, evaluated by Western blotting assay. (e) and (f) Tumor growth curves and survival rates of tumor-bearing mice post various treatments as indicated. The figure was originally published by Tian et al.75 and has been approved for reuse by John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Download figure Download PowerPoint Thus, oxygen nanoshuttles that attenuate tumor hypoxia facilitate safe and efficient chemotherapy of intrinsically chemoresistant solid tumors. Oxygen Nanoshuttles for Enhanced Cancer Immunotherapy Immunotherapy is a promising cancer treatment modality, utilizing the host immune system for potent systemic attack of metastatic tumors.76 Over the past several years, we have witnessed the success of cancer immunotherapies, including chimeric antigen receptor T-cell immunotherapy, as well as immune checkpoint blockade using anti-PD-1/PD-L1 and anti-CTLA-4 antibodies, for the treatment of a wide range of cancers.76–78 However, accumulating clinical data show that chimeric antigen receptor T-cell immunotherapy has limited therapeutic efficacy for treatment of solid tumors, and that checkpoint blockade also shows an average objective response rate of ∼20% in most solid tumors.79 Preclinical and clinical evidence indicate that tumor hypoxia may induce an immunosuppressive TME that limits T-cell infiltration within the hypoxic zones. In addition, the immunosuppressive TME features in remarkably elevated populations of regulatory T cells, M2 macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and myofibroblasts, which prevent tumor cells attack by natural killer and T cells during tumor progression and after chemotherapy or immunotherapy.80 Recently, various nanoparticle-based strategies have also been examined for modulating and diminishing the immunosuppressive TME, and thus enhance immunotherapy.24,25,81 Photodynamic therapy induces release or surface exposure of damage-associated molecular patterns by dying tumor cells, such as ATP, calreticulin, and high-mobility group protein B1.82 These patterns prime the host immune system to generate a systemic attack against residual tumor cells, by promoting maturation of dendritic cells, and subsequent activation of effector T cells and natural killer cells.83 However, this immune priming process is disabled by the hostile TME.83 In recent work by Cai and co-workers,36 a hybrid oxygen nanoshuttle was prepared by cross-linking hemoglobin and reduced HSA, encapsulating Ce6—a photosensitizer that produces singlet oxygen—and subsequently oxygenating the nanoparticles. These Ce6 and oxygen-carrying nanoshuttles enhanced PDT against primary tumors and improved the antitumor immune response against distant tumors and lung metastasis, via enhanced maturation of dendritic cells and activation of effector T cells and natural killer cells. Radiotherapy also induces immunogenic cell death following treatment of tumors.82 We recently found that sequential administration of liposomal catalase and liposomal H2O2 promotes tumor oxygenation of murine breast and colon xenografts, and a patient-derived prostate cancer xenograft20 (Figure 4a–e). Tumor oxygenation reversed the immunosuppressive TME by reducing the M2 macrophage population and improving CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Combining systemic administration of anti-CTLA-4 further enhanced the efficacy of tumor-oxygenation-boosted radiotherapy (Figure 4c–e). Figure 4 | Self-supplied tumor oxygenation with sequential injection of liposomal catalase and H2O2 for enhanced radioimmunotherapy. (a) Scheme showing preparation and mechanism of sequentially injected liposomal catalase and H2O2 for tumor hypoxia attenuation and reversal of immunosuppressive TME, resulting in enhanced cancer radioimmunotherapy. (b) Therapeutic timeline of radioimmunotherapy via sequential injection of liposomal catalase and H2O2, X-ray exposure, and injection of anti-CTLA-4 at indicated time points. (c)–(e) Tumor growth curves, tumor photographs, and average tumor weights after various treatments as indicated. The figure was originally published by Song et al.20 and has been approved for reuse by ACS Publishing group. Download figure Download PowerPoint Therefore, tumor oxygenation is a promising strategy for reversing the immunosuppressive TME and enhancing cancer immunotherapy. Conclusion and Perspectives In this review, we summarized the latest progress in design and fabrication of innovative tumor-targeted oxygen-delivery nanoshuttles. Such dedicated oxygen nanoshuttles were able to efficiently attenuate tumor hypoxia in mouse tumor models, leading to enhanced treatment outcome of oxygen-consuming cancer therapeutics. Moreover, treatment with such oxygen nanoshuttles could reverse the immunosuppressive TME and boost the immune system for enhanced cancer immunotherapy. Thus, oxygen nanoshuttles to promote cancer treatment hold great potential for future clinical translation. However, similar to preceding versions of artificial blood substitutes, concerns regarding biocompatibility of oxygen nanoshuttles remain a prominent obstacle to clinical translation. Circulation half-life of current oxygen nanoshuttles, for sustained oxygenation of primary tumors and the TME, is another key parameter that requires improvement. Tumor hypoxia is associated with tumor acidity, dense extracellular matrix, and high interstitial pressure, which collectively promote the immunosuppressive TME that disables tumor immune surveillance. Therefore, although tumor oxygenation enhances response to therapy, full reversal of therapeutic resistance requires concurrent modulation of other hostile features. Developing multifunctional oxygen nanoshuttles to enable multifaceted TME modulation is a promising future direction for promoting precision cancer nanomedicine.
